title: /HIST 300 Blacks in the United States, 1607-1877
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: CONTENT. Blacks in the United States from the colonial period to 1877. Themes include but are not limited to the slave trade and slavery, resistance to slavery, the significance of slavery in the sectional crisis, the recruitment of Black soldiers and sailors in the Civil War, free blacks and the impact of the Civil War, the destruction of slavery, the Reconstruction Amendments and the impact of Reconstruction on Black Americans. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: HIST 300/AFST 300 .

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 333 ; grade of C or better in ANSC 305 and ANSC 318 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Exercise Physiology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Changes within the systems of the horse resulting from the physical stresses of exercise, adaptations of systems in response to a training regimen; methodology for measuring improvement in physical condition; foundation for development of training programs for horses in moderate, intense or prolonged performance activities. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 333 ; grade of C or better in ANSC 305 and ANSC 318 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification.

description: (ANTH 2346, HUMA 2323) Introduction to Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates anthropology as the holistic and relativistic study of humankind, exploring human life across diverse cultures, time periods and geographical locations. Examines the discipline through its four major subfields: archaeology (the study of material culture and the past), biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), sociocultural anthropology (the study of cultural systems and social organization) and linguistic anthropology (the study of language construction and symbolism). Applies fundamental concepts, including the scientific method and evolutionary theory, to complex human experiences. Develops abilities in critical thinking, analysis of empirical data and effective communication, engaging with culturally diverse and sometimes controversial subjects. Analyzes the discipline’s relationship with society and its impact on global communities over time. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores human evolutionary history, including primate behavior and hominin development; analyzes the history of human biological variation and the lack of a scientific basis for "race"; examines material culture, ancient civilizations and archaeological methods; studies language construction, symbolism and communication patterns; investigates social organization, including kinship, family, marriage and gender; explores economic systems, political structures, religion and belief systems; and applies anthropological thinking to contemporary issues such as, but not limited to, health, medicine, forensics, violence and global challenges. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world; also taught at Qatar campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: (ANTH 2302) Introduction to Archaeology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the basic principles of studying past human cultures through material remains. Surveys the fundamentals of archaeological practice and frameworks, applying interdisciplinary methods to reconstruct and interpret the archaeological record. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces careers in anthropology and archaeology and the skills needed for them. TOPICS AND THEMES. Interdisciplinary nature of archaeological research. Site formation, survival and identification. Field and laboratory methods including survey, excavation, recording, curation and various types of analysis including dating methods. Relationships between humans and environments. Human evolution and behavior including past movement, subsistence strategies, foraging strategies, trade, tool production and development, sedentism, symbolic and ritual behaviors, domestication, city and state formation and reconstruction of past social and individual identities. Archaeological ethics, the role of archaeology in contemporary society and heritage management. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Peoples and Cultures of the World
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys human cultures around the world using case studies of customs and cultural organization. Explores how anthropology is a holistic discipline focused on all of humanity, which integrates knowledge from diverse fields like history, economics, psychology, sociology and traditional sciences. Explores global interconnectedness alongside cultural diversity, addressing questions of "us and them". Develops a greater understanding of the breadth of variation in the human condition and the power of culture to shape individual experience. Recognizes the trade-offs between cultural relativist and universalist perspectives. Gains cultural awareness to inform future evaluations of domestic and global issues. Practices communicating opinions in a culturally respectful manner. Relates outcomes of cultural study to one’s understanding of one’s own culture. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes key anthropological concepts, including fieldwork, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, holism and ethnography. Considers human universals and cultural uniqueness. Studies cultural expressions related to basic perceptions (color, space, distance) and the body (beauty standards, adornment, modification). Explores systems of social organization, including gender, sports, games, communication, gestures and greetings. Investigates cultural practices concerning food, eating, reciprocity, trade, etiquette, folklore and magic. Examines cultural approaches to death, dying, medicine, illness and health.

subject: ANTH
title: Cross Cultural Competency
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops skills vital for effective engagement in an increasingly diverse and interconnected world. Fosters personal awareness of biases, attitudes, values, beliefs and ways of knowing (epistemology). Explores the profound impact of culture on the ability to think critically and communicate effectively. Trains students to critically appraise how their worldview and life experiences shape the decisions they make. Synthesizes core concepts like culture, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, stereotypes, worldview and holism, applying them to the student's chosen discipline or subject of interest. Promotes enhanced self-knowledge and cross-cultural awareness through active, reflexive inquiry. Encourages challenging one's own thinking, especially when subject matter elicits an emotional reaction, to ensure critical engagement with evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes fundamental concepts in anthropology, including culture, diversity, race and ethnicity. Consideration of holism and reductionism in understanding systems and thought processes. Explores personal learning styles, personality strengths and systems of knowledge (epistemology). Examines communication dynamics, ethnocentrism, stereotypes, myths, fallacies and assumptions. Discusses ethical frameworks, including critical cultural relativism. Studies critical thinking skills applicable across varied professional, cultural and scientific contexts.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
prereq_text: Concurrent registration in ANTH 226 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: (ANTH 2301, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates human biology and evolution by exploring the origins of humanity through evolutionary processes and the Primate fossil record. Analyzes the mechanisms of evolutionary change, such as human genetics and heredity, that shape human populations and non-human primate diversity. Trains students to ask how shared evolutionary history influences modern human adaptation and variation, gaining a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Discussion addresses the genetic and environmental basis of human biological variation, our relationship to other primates and the fossil record associated with our extinct hominin relatives/ancestors. Writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students' critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers evolutionary processes acting on modern and ancient human populations; analyzes human genetics, heredity and molecular biology; studies non-human Primate anatomy, fossil record, classification, behavior and ecology; methods used to study the fossil record including comparative anatomy, taphonomy, basic fieldwork protocols and age estimation techniques; examines the human fossil record, including our earliest possible relatives, the Australopithecines, and species in the genus Homo; explores contemporary human biological variation, anatomy, adaptation, health and forensic anthropology; develops skills in critical thinking, inquiry and analysis of relevant sources. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 226 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Cultural Change and Development
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates the broad spectrum of cultural dynamics, providing an overview of how societies transform and adapt through cultural change. Examines diverse methodologies and theoretical approaches used to document and interpret these shifts. Draws on case studies and source materials from all areas of anthropology, integrating knowledge from allied fields. Develops a strong understanding of the complexities inherent in cultural change. Enhances the ability to employ theoretical concepts in novel and innovative ways. Clarifies the practical need to apply anthropological knowledge in programs of directed change. Encourages respectful critique and defense of diverse points of view regarding current social issues. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies the fundamental concept of culture; analyzes definitions, overviews and data sources related to cultural change; investigates dynamic processes such as innovation, diffusion and acculturation; considers theoretical approaches including functionalism, cultural materialism and cultural evolution; examines maladaptive traits and Darwinian evolutionary principles applied to culture; explores the intersection of cultural change and health; and analyzes colonial legacies and the dynamics of directed change.

subject: ANTH
title: North American Archaeology
prereq_text: ANTH 201 , ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 , ANTH 205 , or ANTH 210 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology of North America from the first arrival of humans on the continent through recent historical archaeology. Emphasis will be upon the geographic area of the continental United States and Canada, with a focus on past Indigenous lifeways and their variation in time and in space. Discusses individual sites and places them into their regional context. Develops critical analysis skills of the lines of evidence most common to North American archaeology, including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies and social and individual identities of past people of North America. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include the concept of culture areas and its evolution over time, environmental archaeology, migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, warfare, culture contact, archaeological laws, ethics and politics, including the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act and Indigenous archaeology in North America. The course will include historical archaeology but focuses upon pre-European archaeology. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including paleoenvironmental proxies, material culture analysis, iconography, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of North American societies and their rich, complex histories. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to North American archaeology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 201 , ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 , ANTH 205 , or ANTH 210 .

subject: ANTH
title: Mesoamerican Archaeology
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 , or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the peoples and civilizations of Mesoamerica—a cultural region encompassing the southern two-thirds of Mexico and the northern half of Central America, including present-day Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador and northwestern Honduras. Traces the full arc of human occupation in the region, from the earliest settlements over 14,000 years ago to the arrival of Europeans in the 15th century. Critically evaluates archaeological data and interpretations and situates Mesoamerican case studies within broader anthropological and theoretical frameworks. TOPICS AND THEMES. Emphasizing critical engagement with key debates in Mesoamerican archaeology, the course examines topics such as the origins of agriculture and urbanism, household and state economies, social stratification, ritual and religion, warfare, mobility and migration, and processes of collapse and resilience. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including ancient DNA, material culture analysis, iconography, writing systems, linguistics, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of Mesoamerican societies and their rich, complex histories. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 , or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Fossil Evidence of Human Evolution
prereq_text: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human evolution from the time of divergence from the other African apes through the appearance of anatomically modern humans. Delves into the detailed study of the fossil antecedents of humans. Applies fundamental principles from evolutionary biology, geology, primatology and paleontology to interpret the human lineage. Integrates evidence from the human fossil record, archaeological material, ancient DNA and living human populations. Studies comparative osteology and paleoecology to interpret the evolutionary relationships, diet and behavior of extinct and living human and non-human Primate species. Analyzes the evolutionary mechanisms that have patterned life on Earth and the forces that have acted upon these processes. Develops a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Develops a comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary mechanisms that position humans within the larger Primate clade and the genetic and environmental underpinnings of modern human variability and dispersal. Hands-on, discussion and writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students’ critical reading/thinking skills and apply paleoanthropological methods to real and modeled skeletal materials. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers human evolutionary biology, including evolutionary processes, natural selection and macroevolutionary principles. Analyses geological and paleontological contexts, focusing on fossils, taphonomy and dating techniques. Examines living and extinct primate diversity and evolution, covering early primates and apes. Studies specific hominin species, including the earliest possible hominins, Australopithecus, Paranthropus, Homo species (such as H. erectus, H. naledi and H. neanderthalensis) and Homo sapiens. Investigates comparative morphology, osteology and diagnostic skeletal features of the human skeleton. Explores and describes paleoecology, anatomy, diet, human evolutionary trends and the genetic and environmental underpinnings that have shaped our species. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Historical Archaeology
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the material and documentary evidence of European colonization in North America and its impact on Indigenous populations, African enslaved peoples and the environment. Integrates historical records with archaeological findings to understand how European imperial powers such as the Spanish, the Basques, the French, the Dutch and the English shaped the Americas through settlement, trade and social structures. Includes case studies from contact-era settlements, plantations, forts, battlefields and maritime contexts, highlighting how artifacts, architecture and written documents complement and sometimes challenge one another. Emphasizes methods of historical archaeology, including document transcription, genealogical research, artifact analysis and field methods that provide students with tools to critically interpret North American history through a material lens. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in historical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. European exploration and colonial expansion led by European nations including Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England; Indigenous populations; forced migration and enslavement of Africans; trade, exchange and economic structures; archaeology of gender, identity, racialization, plantations, forts, battlefields, settlements, graves and shipwrecks; historical archaeological theory and methods including survey and excavation methods, absolute and relative dating methods and artifact analysis; archival and research skills including genealogical research, transcription and historical document analysis; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Ships and Shipwrecks of the Americas
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how ships and seafaring shaped the history and culture of the Western Hemisphere from 1492 through the American Civil War. Draws on archaeological discoveries and historical records to examine exploration, colonization, trade, naval conflict and technological innovation through the lens of maritime material culture. Reviews case studies of shipwrecks and other maritime sites, revealing the vessels, technologies and practices that connected cultures, facilitated economic systems and transformed warfare. From Indigenous watercraft to colonial gunboats, steamboats and Civil War submarines, engages with the archaeological evidence that illuminates change and continuity in the maritime world of the Americas. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology of the Americas. TOPICS AND THEMES. Ship construction; ship rigging; seafaring technologies; European and American shipwreck archaeological case studies; Iberian voyages of exploration; Basque whaling; Spain’s maritime empire; Northern European maritime exploration; colonization; technological developments; economics and history of the Western Hemisphere; European-Indigenous relationships; Indigenous watercraft; Anglo-French wars; piracy and privateering; Revolutionary War; War of 1812; Shipping in the Commercial Age; canal transport; horse-powered boats; steamboats; packet ships; clipper ships; whaling fleets; Arctic exploration; Civil War naval warfare. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys seafaring and maritime culture in the Mediterranean from the Stone Age through the Roman Republic, with an excursus on fluvial galleys of Imperial Rome. Examines the archaeological and historical evidence for ancient navigation, shipbuilding and maritime trade, with a focus on both land-based and underwater sites. Students explore Egyptian seafaring on the Nile and in the Red Sea, Bronze Age shipwrecks such as Uluburun and Cape Gelidonya, Phoenician and Greek colonization, Etruscan maritime activity and Roman naval and merchant vessels. subject: ANTH
title: European Archaeology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of human prehistory and history on the European continent and surrounding islands through the remains of material culture such as artifacts, human and animal remains, structures, landscapes and environments. Investigates the wide time span from the earliest Paleolithic hunter-gatherer hominids (up to two million years ago), through the Neolithic agricultural “revolution”, the metal ages, the classical civilizations of Greece and Rome, the medieval period and up to the modern era. Develops critical analysis skills using different types of information including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources to understand individual sites. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies, and social and individual identities of past Europeans. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include human origins and migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, urbanization and state formation including hunter-gatherers, small scale societies, cities and empires; conflict and warfare; religion and ritual; art, music and culture; social, cultural and individual identity. Methodologies discussed include archaeological excavations, surveys, GIS, spatial analysis, analysis of landscapes and buildings, dating methods, artifact analysis, examination of human and animal remains, environmental and geoarchaeology, lab methods including ancient DNA, proteins, lipids, and stable isotopes, ethnographies and experimental archaeology. Class discussions may be thought-provoking and introduce new perspectives and material that students may not have encountered before. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 353 Archaeology of Ancient Greece
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 353/ANTH 353 .

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 354 Archaeology of Ancient Italy
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Italy from the Stone Age through the collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Students examine the material culture, art and architecture of the Etruscans and Romans, as well as the prehistoric and early Italic foundations that shaped them. Explores how Italy’s peoples expressed identity, religion and power through sculpture, painting, mosaics, inscriptions, temples, homes and civic monuments. Special emphasis is placed on the development of Rome from a small city-state into a vast imperial capital, the role of urbanism and daily life, and the ways in which material remains reveal both continuity and transformation across centuries of Italian history. TOPICS AND THEMES. Prehistoric Italy and the Stone Age; Villanovans and the emergence of the Etruscans; Etruscan cities and art; early Rome and urban foundations; Romanization and the Republic; Augustan classicism; imperial art and architecture under the Julio-Claudians, Flavians and Antonines; wall painting, mosaics and domestic life; Pompeii and Herculaneum; the lure of the games and public spectacles; baths, theaters and civic monuments; coinage and inscriptions as evidence of social and political life; Ostia and imperial urbanism; ships and shipwrecks of Roman Italy; Severan and Late Roman art; Constantine and the transformation of Roman identity; collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 354/ANTH 354 .

subject: ANTH
title: Ancient Civilizations of the World
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores archaeological studies that have contributed to our understanding of the emergence and decline of states and civilizations between 3500 BCE and 1500 CE. Examines the complex origins of anthropology and archaeology within the discourses on "civilization" and comparative models of human development. Explores the political organization, social structures, cultural practices and technological advancements of complex societies in regions such as the Near East, Africa, Europe, India, China, Mesoamerica and North America. Explores theoretical frameworks, methodological approaches and the interpretation of archaeological and related data to comprehend the nature of these complex societies in various parts of the world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Theories of civilization and socio-political organization of ancient societies, neo-evolutionary models of social complexity, agricultural societies and the rise of states, archaeological evidence of hierarchy, heterarchy, urbanism, and state formation in ancient societies, environmental factors in the rise and fall of complex societies; trade, warfare and cooperation in ancient societies; comparative studies of complex societies, states and empires in various regions of the world; the collapse of ancient states and lessons for modern states. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Ice Age Humans in the Americas
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or equivalent.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines archaeological, environmental, geological and genetic evidence related to the timing of human entry into the Americas and megafaunal extinctions at the end of the Pleistocene. Engages students in the most recent findings from archaeological sites across the Americas. In this class students learn to evaluate evidence critically and synthesize the most up to date information on human dispersals in the western hemisphere at the end of the last Ice Age. TOPICS AND THEMES. Chronology and migration routes of early settlement; environmental and landscape change, important archeological sites in North, Central and South America, controversial claims and standards of evidence, theories of forager mobility and landscape learning and current methods accelerating the pace of discoveries. Prerequisite: ANTH 202 or equivalent.

subject: ANTH
title: Archaeological Artifact Conservation
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and practice of conserving archaeological artifacts, emphasizing the stabilization and long-term preservation of materials recovered from terrestrial and underwater sites. Examines both theoretical grounding and extensive hands-on experience in the laboratory, learning to assess artifact condition, select appropriate treatment strategies and apply conservation techniques to a wide range of materials including organics, ceramics, glass and metals. Through lectures, readings and laboratory exercises, students explore the chemical and physical principles underlying conservation, the ethical considerations surrounding intervention and preservation and the role of conservation within archaeological research and curation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Principles of archaeological conservation and preservation; conservation ethics and documentation; health and safety in the conservation laboratory; adhesives and consolidants; conservation of organic materials including bone, ivory, wood, leather, textiles and rope; stabilization of siliceous materials such as ceramics, glass and stone; corrosion processes and treatment of archaeological metals including iron, copper alloys, lead, tin and precious metals; electrolytic and chemical cleaning methods; desalinization and drying processes; material identification and condition assessment; factors of decay in burial environments; field conservation practices; reconstruction techniques and aesthetic reintegration; and integration of conservation data into archaeological interpretation and collections management. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 403 Anthropology of Religion
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: RELS 403/ANTH 403 .

subject: ANTH
title: Science, Pseudoscience and Critical Thinking in Anthropology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examination of extraordinary claims made across a wide spectrum of media in the fields of anthropology, biological anthropology and archaeology. Emphasis on distinguishing science from pseudoscience through application of the scientific method, logical reasoning and critical evaluation of empirical evidence. Writing-intensive assignments develop students’ critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively about complex and sometimes controversial issues in anthropology and in broader scientific inquiry. Attention to recognizing and refuting poor scientific reasoning, evaluation of media portrayal of science and clear dissemination of ideas within and beyond academic contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of science, pseudoscience, pathological science, junk science and anti-science; scientific hoaxes, frauds and exaggeration of evidence; the scientific method and the use and misuse of statistics and illustrations; distortions of anthropological and scientific knowledge across a variety of media platforms, including social media and ‘fake news’; history of the discipline of anthropology; IQ testing, race, and racism; creation science, natural selection, and evolution; cryptozoology, bigfoot and aquatic apes; the use, misuse and abuse of the archaeological record in both scientific and popular discourse; the supernatural realm; and conspiracy theories, climate science and vaccine efficacy. Course discussions may also engage diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting a variety of contexts – scientific, professional, political, cultural – in which group communication occurs. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropological Theory
prereq_text: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the history and foundations of anthropological theory, connecting these historical concepts to contemporary professional concerns. Critiques the core assumptions, preferred questions and specific methods associated with major theoretical schools. Engages diverse points of view to examine current social issues and applied problems, fostering respect for cultural and human biological diversity. Develops comprehensive expertise in articulating theoretical explanations for research questions, identifying the major theorist(s) credited for theory development and detailing how theory is currently used by anthropologists. Practices critical synthesis of theoretical knowledge within existing disciplinary frameworks. Evaluates arguments by questioning the type and sufficiency of evidence presented. Assesses the cultural position, background and historical context of authors conveying messages, including whether the argument is shaped by a particular historical moment or if the author has an agenda. Requires active application of theoretical models against individual student areas of interest. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores foundational classics; analyzes epistemology, axiology and related conceptual frameworks; considers the Nature/Nurture Debate; investigation of functional thinking, processes, structures and pragmatics; transformation and evolution; symbols and coherence; cultural materialism and economies; and critical advocacy, feminisms, Post Modernism, post-structuralism and the ontological turn. Prerequisite: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205 .

subject: ANTH
title: Archaeological Theory
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. An advanced undergraduate course reviewing the history of scientific archaeological thought, major theoretical paradigms and current trends in archaeology, provides firm grounding in the development and current application of archaeological theory, a fundamental component of all students’ training in archaeology, no matter their specialty. Covers the major theoretical “movements” in the development of anthropological archaeology, as well as important intellectual developments in other disciplines which have influenced explanation in archaeology (e.g., cultural anthropology, geology, evolutionary biology and other social sciences). Historically oriented, reviews how archaeological theory has evolved in the past century and how contemporary archaeologists use theory to explain variability in the material-culture record of past humans. TOPICS AND THEMES. History of scientific archaeological exploration; major theoretical paradigms and movements in archaeological theory; current trends in archaeology; intellectual developments from other disciplines that influenced archaeological thought. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropological Writing
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Practices critical reading and writing skills through the study and discussion of anthropologically relevant literature. Examines various styles and formats of anthropological writing, treating the discipline as an ongoing conversation and discourse community. Develops writing proficiency necessary for professional participation in anthropology and related career paths, including the interpretation, critique and evaluation of scientific papers. Emphasizes effective peer review and the capacity to accept constructive criticism. Cultivates clear communication strategies for discussing complex anthropological topics with both academic and broader audiences. Organizes written work using careful and critical thought. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers common citation styles, including the appropriate inclusion of primary sources. Analyzes the scientific publication process and Reference Management Software (RMS) usage. Studies professional writing, including personal statements, cover letters, CVs and resumes, prepared as part of an application packet for jobs, internships or graduate school. Explores writing clearly and concisely for diverse audiences, including rewriting scholarly work for non-academic audiences and developing an original research paper on a topic of the student’s choosing. Examines various styles of scientific papers, including research articles, review articles, programmatic essays, ethnographies and popular media. Practices peer review techniques and critical analysis of complex texts. Verbal communication and synthesis of anthropological research in small group settings and an individual oral presentation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 417 Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 417/ANTH 417 .

subject: ANTH
title: Romans, Arabs, and Vikings--Seafaring in the Mediterranean during the early Christian Era
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Examination of seafaring, maritime commerce, naval affairs, and shipbuilding in the Mediterranean from the late Roman Period until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Pirates, Privateers and Sea Raiders
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth survey of the history and archaeology of piracy, privateering and sea raiding from ancient times in the eastern Mediterranean through the Viking Era in the Northern Atlantic and the rise of piracy in the New World and Caribbean during the 16th–18th centuries. Examines archaeological evidence of pirate ventures, the social organization of pirate and privateering communities and the economic, political and cultural effects of piracy on empires, trade networks and maritime law. Explores the sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music, and introduces contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Through lectures, readings, presentations and research assignments, students develop critical skills to evaluate primary and secondary sources, analyze cause-and-effect relationships and assess the broader impact of piracy across time and regions. TOPICS. May include: origins, causes and major periods of piracy, privateering and sea raiding; archaeological evidence of pirate activity in the Mediterranean, Northern Atlantic, Caribbean and Americas; Viking, European and New World piracy; raids, privateering and colonial interactions; social structure, codes of conduct and daily life of pirate communities; economic and political effects of piracy on trade, colonialism, slavery and national sovereignty; sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music; cultural responses to piracy; female pirates and gender dynamics in seafaring communities; contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia; case studies of shipwrecks, pirate lairs and maritime settlements; research methods and critical evaluation of primary and secondary sources. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: /MUST 421 Advanced Museum Studies
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MUST 221 , ANTH 221 , ARCH 221 or MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Advanced exploration of historical, political and cultural forces shaping contemporary museum practices and exhibition design, with emphasis on ethical and professional responsibilities in modern institutions. Focuses on the collaborative and interdisciplinary processes behind exhibition planning and production, with attention to visitor experience, inclusive design and object-based interpretation. Critically engages with contemporary challenges in the museum field, including representation, decolonization, repatriation, activism, censorship and institutional accountability. Highlights the museum’s role in public service, education, knowledge advancement and civic discourse. Includes field trips to campus and local museums, archives and historical or cultural institutions to support experiential learning and engagement with professional practices and careers. Fulfills core requirement for the Museum Studies Minor. Topics and themes may include: Historical and contemporary models of museum programming; research methodologies and scholarly use of collections; educational theory and practice in museum contexts; public outreach and community engagement; ethics of representation, access and inclusion; museums and democratic ideals, civic responsibility and public trust; professional standards and leadership in museum operations; critical evaluation of exhibitions and interpretive strategies; responsive programming tied to current events and emerging issues. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MUST 221 , ANTH 221 , ARCH 221 or MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: MUST 421/ANTH 421 .

subject: ANTH
title: Human Osteology
prereq_text: ANTH 225 and ANTH 226 , or VIBS 305 ; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores human osteological analysis, which provides fundamental skills for fields such as bioarchaeology, paleontology, biomechanics, human anatomy and forensic anthropology. Investigates the concepts and methods anthropologists employ to identify, describe and analyze skeletal remains from archaeological and forensic contexts. Trains students in the proper use of anatomical terminology and the respectful handling of human remains. Intensive hands-on activities develop and apply essential skills in identifying and siding core skeletal elements and teeth. Focuses on how the human skeleton functions, grows and changes throughout the lifespan. Addresses the possibilities and limitations of anthropological skeletal analysis and the ethical concerns inherent in modern osteological study. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies skeletal and dental biology, including gross and microscopic bone and tooth structure. Analyses effects of ontogeny, development and age on the skeletal system. Estimates parameters such as sex, age, ancestry, stature, anomalies and pathologies of human skeletal remains using standardized anthropological methods. Considers pathological analysis, dietary reconstruction and comparison with faunal remains. Examines cultural, occupational and postmortem modifications, including taphonomy. Reviews methods used in initial assessment, inventory and recovery of remains. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 and ANTH 226 , or VIBS 305 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropology of Human Reproduction
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human courtship, marriage, reproduction, family structure and parenting through the lens of evolutionary ecology. Explores how human reproductive and parenting patterns compare with those of other primates and how they vary across cultures. Evaluates different viewpoints on and approaches to the application of evolutionary logic to the study of these topics. Critically examines hypotheses explaining human behavior through biological, cultural and ecological lenses. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include evolutionary approaches to the study of human behavior, life histories, reproductive strategies, sexual selection, marriage, parental care, infidelity, divorce, as well as explorations of cross-cultural and cross-species variation in these areas. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Medical Anthropology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Ethnobotany
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the dynamic relationships between people and plants through the interdisciplinary lens of ethnobotany. Introduces the field by examining how disciplines such as botany, anthropology, ethnopharmacology, ethnoecology and ethnomedicine contribute to understanding plant use across cultures. Engages critically with foundational concepts, including plant adaptations for defense, human strategies for utilizing those adaptations, diverse ways of knowing and the development of knowledge systems that codify plant use. Emphasizes analytical and methodological inquiry into how plant ecosystems and knowledge systems shape human-plant interactions. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies plant structures, functions and identification using botanical methods; analyzes traditional ecological knowledge and cognitive ethnobotany through ethnographic and comparative approaches; considers ethnopharmacological practices including tinctures, infusions and salves with attention to preparation and efficacy; explores sensory and perceptual ecology using qualitative and observational techniques; examines ethnoecology and conservation strategies through field-based and participatory methods; investigates ethnomedicine, medical models and health conditions using cross-cultural and clinical perspectives; and evaluates ethical issues in research and practice through case studies and applied frameworks. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 438 Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline
prereq_text: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 438/ANTH 438 .

subject: ANTH
title: Lithic Artifact Analysis
prereq_text: ANTH 202 and approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
description: Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis. Prerequisite: ANTH 202 and approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Quantitative Methods in Anthropology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Presents practical training in statistics applicable to anthropological and archaeological data. Provides anthropology students with the sophisticated statistical skills needed for an increasingly quantitative field. Discusses reasons why anthropological and archaeological data does not always meet the criteria set by many formal statistical models. Teaches the methods to analyze the chronological, geographic, morphometric, demographic, phylogenetic, genetic, linguistic, network/interaction and observational datasets (among others) that pose unique challenges for both analysis and interpretation. Conducts scientific statistical analyses of these datasets. Applies statistical concepts and techniques to real and hypothetical anthropological or archaeological problems during weekly lab sections. TOPICS AND THEMES. Quantitative analytical methods employed by anthropologists; includes statistical analyses, statistical software and sampling theory commonly used in anthropological research. Graphical techniques and statistics specific to anthropological datasets and research questions, including exploratory data analysis (e.g. principal components, canonical variates, factor analysis), and other multivariate methods (e.g. MANOVA). This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303 .

subject: ANTH
title: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces quantitative ethnographic field methods commonly used in anthropological research to formally test hypotheses. Explores the benefits and challenges of applying structured, quantitative techniques to the study of complex cultural phenomena within a field largely dominated by qualitative methods. Covers best practices for managing and analyzing anthropological datasets. Surveys common ethnographic methods designed to enhance comparability and analytical rigor of ethnographic research, including structured interviews, text analysis and network analysis. Through hands-on assignments, provides practical experience in developing and executing small-scale research projects. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include ethical considerations in field research, research design, data management, statistical analysis, structured interviews, online survey tools, standardized observation, network analysis, text analysis and cultural consensus analysis. Also includes student participation in all stages of the research process, including research design, data collection, data management and analysis, and write-up. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Environmental Archaeology
prereq_text: ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science. TOPICS AND THEMES. The use of archaeological sites as paleoenvironmental archives, human impacts on ancient environments, Quaternary extinctions, long-term landscape evolution, plant and animal domestication, the Anthropocene and cultural collapse and resilience. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

subject: ARCH
title: Foundations of Museum Studies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums. Cross Listing: ANTH 221 and MUST 221 .

subject: ARCH
title: Elements of Urban Design
prereq_text: Admission to upper level division in BED or BS-URPN.
description: Investigation of design elements shaping the urban environment; emphasis placed on contemporary precedents in architecture, landscape and urbanism to evaluate design complexity on multiple levels: social, political, environmental, economic, cultural and geographic. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level division in BED or BS-URPN.

subject: ARCH
title: Energy and Sustainable Architecture
prereq_text: Junior and senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Understanding the various design decisions impacting sustainability and energy efficiency; includes participation in an "academic" LEED-NC rating project; interdisciplinary team approach with a design studio architect to perform the LEED-NC rating on the architect's building; application of reference material, standards, and USGBC material. Prerequisite: Junior and senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ARCH
title: History of Ancient Architecture in the Near East, Egypt, Greece and Rome
prereq_text: ARCH 249 or ARTS 149 ; junior or senior classification or approval of degree coordinator or instructor.
description: Examination of stylistic, structural and theoretical advancements in ancient architecture, with case studies from the Near East, Egypt, Greece and Rome. Prerequisite: ARCH 249 or ARTS 149 ; junior or senior classification or approval of degree coordinator or instructor.

Prerequisite: ARCH 250 or ARTS 150 ; junior or senior classification or approval of degree coordinator or instructor.

prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor or degree coordinator.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253, or equivalent, or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 ; grade of C or better in ENGR 216/PHYS 216 or PHYS 216/ENGR 216 .
description: Principles of statics, kinematics, and kinetics, with particular attention to architectural engineering applications; general principles of mechanics; concurrent force systems; statics of particles; equivalent force/moment systems; centroids and center of gravity; equilibrium of rigid bodies; trusses, and frames; internal forces in structural members; friction; second moments of areas; force action related to displacement, velocity, and acceleration of rigid bodies; kinematics of plane motion; kinetics of translation and rotation; mass moment of inertia; vibration; work, energy, and power; impulse and momentum. title: Contemporary Issues in Science - Cosmos, Earth and Humanity
description: This team-taught, interdisciplinary course builds scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues — current questions, discoveries and challenges at the intersection of science and society. Topics may include the Big Bang, evolution, genetics, human reproduction and health, vaccines, drugs, artificial intelligence, cryptography and cybersecurity. subject: ASIA
title: /HIST 352 Modern East Asia
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: CONTENT. Examination of East Asia (broadly conceived) and its history in the modern era. Topics include, but are not limited to, the transformation from premodern societies to modernity; East Asian encounters with Western imperialism; nationalism and the formation of modern states; wars and conflicts; economic, social, cultural and political developments; and intra-Asian interactions as well as engagements with the wider world. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: HIST 352/ASIA 352 .

subject: BESC
title: Biotechnology for Biofuels and Bioproducts
prereq_text: BESC 201 and junior or senior classification.
description: This course explores the scientific and technological foundations of bioenergy. Students will critically analyze feedstocks across the three major generations of biofuels, assessing their unique characteristics, applications and limitations. Key enabling technologies — including pretreatment methods, fermentation processes and conversion pathways — are examined in depth. The course covers topics such as ethanol, biodiesel, biogas, biohydrogen and other emerging biofuels and bioproducts, reinforced through case studies and applied quantitative analyses of yield and productivity. Broader discussions and projects highlight recent advances in bioenergy research and the integration of biorefinery concepts, preparing students to critically assess the challenges and opportunities of the field. Prerequisites: BESC 201 and junior or senior classification.

subject: BESC
title: U.S. Environmental Regulations
prereq_text: BESC 201 , ENSS 105 or RWFM 308 .
description: This course provides an overview of the U.S. legal infrastructure regulating environmental impacts. Students will explore core legal and scientific terminology, historical developments and the core role of the EPA. Major regulations of key statutes addressing air and water quality, waste management, hazardous substances, energy and natural resources are examined in detail. Emphasis is placed on the rationale behind environmental regulations and the regulatory process. Additional topics include the role of science in shaping policy and the influence of international agreements and environmental justice. Through case studies and projects, students evaluate the effectiveness of environmental regulations in addressing real-world challenges. Prerequisites: BESC 201 , ENSS 105 or RWFM 308 .

subject: BESC
title: Microbial Processes in Bioremediation
prereq_text: CHEM 222 or CHEM 227 .
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles and applications of bioremediation as a sustainable approach to managing contaminated environments. Students will investigate common and emerging environmental contaminants, the critical factors influencing microbial activity, and conduct an in-depth analysis of the microbial metabolic pathways involved in contaminant degradation. Both in-situ and ex-situ bioremediation technologies are explored, alongside complementary physicochemical remediation processes. Through real-world case studies and applied projects, students evaluate recent advances in bioremediation pathways and innovative technologies. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the necessary knowledge and analytical skills to evaluate effective strategies for environmental restoration. Prerequisite: CHEM 222 or CHEM 227 .

subject: BESC
title: Sampling and Environmental Monitoring
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: This course integrates the principles and practices of environmental sampling and monitoring, focusing equally on theory and hands-on application. Students will examine the fundamentals of environmental monitoring and data analysis, pollutant chemistry, regulatory frameworks and Phase I Environmental Site Assessments. Building on this foundation, the course delves into sampling approaches and methodologies for environmental analysis using both in-situ and ex-situ analytical techniques. A dedicated laboratory component provides essential hands-on experience through projects that reinforce concepts, good laboratory practices, quality control and data interpretation. The course culminates with comprehensive capstone experiences, enabling students to apply their knowledge to real-world environmental challenges. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Study of modern genetics with an emphasis on biomedical and health-related applications of the mammalian genome. Topics include classical Mendelian inheritance, pedigree and genetic risk analysis, population genetics, quantitative genetics and the molecular basis of gene structure and function, including DNA replication, transcription, mutation and gene regulation. The course examines how genetic variation and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to disease and phenotypic diversity, and introduces advanced concepts in cytogenetics, epigenetics, cancer genetics and genomics. Contemporary applications such as genome sequencing, gene therapy, personalized medicine and associated ethical considerations are also addressed. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 315, GENE-320 or BIMS-320. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: GENE 320/BIMS 320 .

subject: BIMS
title: Equine-Assisted Activities and Therapies - Best Practices
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Course explores equine assisted services (EAS) best practices, including: principles of EAS, horse welfare, safety factors, effective techniques to promote healing of participants, and career options. Upon completion of this course, students will have demonstrated the ability to define what constitutes a safe and effective EAS program and outline a business model for such a program. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: BIMS
title: /GENE 405 Mammalian Genetics
prereq_text: GENE 302 , BIMS 320/GENE 320 or GENE 320/BIMS 320 ; junior or senior classification in biomedical sciences, genetics, biochemistry and biology.
description: Emphasis on current research and technology application in comparative mammalian genetics and genomics including advanced reproduction technologies and cloning, animal models of disease, biodiversity and functional genetics, cancer genetics, conservation, coat color genetics, cytogenetics, development and stem cells, domestication, epigenetics and gene regulation, forensics applications, genomic medicine, genomics and computational analysis, sex determination and sex chromosomes. Prerequisites: GENE 302 , BIMS 320/GENE 320 or GENE 320/BIMS 320 ; junior or senior classification in biomedical sciences, genetics, biochemistry and biology. Cross Listing: GENE 405/BIMS 405 .

subject: BIMS
title: /GENE 421 Advanced Human Genetics
prereq_text: GENE 302 ; BICH 410 or BICH 440 .
description: A rigorous, analytical approach to genetic analysis of humans including diagnosis and management of genetic disease in humans; transmission of genes in human populations; human cytogenetics; the structure of human genes; human gene mapping; molecular analysis of genetic disease; genetics screening and counseling. Prerequisites: GENE 302 ; BICH 410 or BICH 440 . Cross Listing: GENE 421/BIMS 421 .

subject: BIOL
title: Essentials in Biology
description: (BIOL 1308, BIOL 1408) Essentials in Biology. One-semester biology for non-majors; overview of essential biological concepts and their application to real world and contemporary issues; topics include evolution, biodiversity, cellular, molecular and forensic biology, genetics and heredity to scientific literacy, human impact on the environment, genetically modified organisms and emerging diseases.

title: Introductory Microbiology
prereq_text: BIOL 101 , BIOL 107 , BIOL 111 , or BIOL 113 ; CHEM 119 . May not be used for credit by biology, molecular and cell biology, microbiology, zoology, predentistry or premedicine majors.
description: (BIOL 2320 and 2120, BIOL 2321 and 2121, BIOL 2420, BIOL 2421) Introductory Microbiology. subject: BIOL
title: Molecular Cell Biology
prereq_text: BIOL 112 and CHEM 120 .
description: This course covers how cells are built, powered and regulated. Topics include macromolecules; membranes and transport; energy production and conversion; genome organization and evolution; DNA structure and replication; gene expression and regulation; intracellular trafficking; cytoskeleton; cell communication and electrical signaling; cell division and cancer. Additional topics may be presented based on time and instructor expertise. The course emphasizes evidence-based reasoning, quantitative skills and core experimental methods. Prerequisites: BIOL 112 and CHEM 120 .

subject: BUSN
title: Machine Learning and Predictive Modeling for Business Applications
prereq_text: Artificial Intelligence in Business minor; junior or senior classification.
description: This course helps bridge machine learning concepts with real-world business applications. It covers fundamental machine learning concepts needed to become both an informed user of machine learning/AI products and an effective business project leader. The course develops essential knowledge and skills for working in and managing machine learning projects in the business context. No advanced technical expertise is required. Prerequisites: Artificial Intelligence in Business minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: BUSN
title: Agentic AI in Business
prereq_text: Artificial Intelligence in Business minor; junior or senior classification.
description: This course explores the emerging field of autonomous, goal-driven artificial intelligence systems that can reason, plan and act with minimal human intervention. Students will learn the foundations of agent design, examine real-world applications across industries and critically assess both the opportunities and challenges of deploying agentic AI in business and society. Prerequisites: Artificial Intelligence in Business minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: CARC
title: Cultural and Social Issues in the Natural, Built and Virtual Environment
description: Introduction to cultural and social issues in planning, design, construction, creativity and the visual arts; explores historical and social ways individual and collective values, beliefs and policies are manifested in architecture, landscape architecture, urban planning, construction science and the arts. Emphasizes student-led discussion of topics that relate to social issues and the built environment, such as housing, gentrification, environmental justice, public monuments and memorials, labor force issues in the built environment industries and other contemporary issues. Strengthens students’ communication skills through emphasis on civil discourse, reflection and collaboration in a multicultural society.

subject: CHEM
title: Molecular Science for Citizens
description: (CHEM 1305, 1405*) Molecular Science for Citizens. subject: CLAS
title: History of Christianity I - Origins to the Reformation
description: CONTENT. History of Christianity from its inception until the beginnings of European colonial expansion in the first half of the 16th century. Themes include the teachings of Jesus and his disciples; the growth of Christianity as it spread throughout the Mediterranean basin into Mesopotamia, Africa, Northern Europe and central Asia; variations in doctrinal development and religious practice in diverse social, political and geographical situations. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Cross Listing: HIST 220 and RELS 220 .
