subject: COMM
title: Communication in Health Care Contexts
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how communication functions across health care settings, including interpersonal interactions, organizational systems and/or public messaging. Explores approaches to patient-provider dialogue, teamwork and/or institutional communication, alongside principles used in health campaigns and information dissemination. Addresses how communication practices influence access, understanding, decision-making and/or coordination. Course material may involve discussion of sensitive health topics, addressed for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices applicable to professional effectiveness in clinical, nonprofit, corporate and public-facing health roles. Develops analytical tools for evaluating message strategies, assessing interactional dynamics and interpreting communication within institutional structures. Supports preparation for advanced study in fields related to health, communication or organizational practice, as well as for participation in public discourse surrounding health issues. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how communication in health care involves more than information delivery, incorporating factors such as context, perception, institutional procedures and interpersonal dynamics. Informs understanding of how misunderstandings emerge and ways different approaches to communication may facilitate or impede clarity, coordination and trust. Considers communication as a process with measurable effects. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of physician-patient interaction; health literacy and information accessibility; teamwork and coordination in clinical settings; communication breakdowns and system-level challenges; message design and campaign strategy; risk communication; digital health platforms and telemedicine; confidentiality, regulation and public messaging. Course material may reference real-world health controversies or policy debates as useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Media, Health and Medicine
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how health, illness and medical practice are represented across media environments, including news, social media, entertainment, advertising and/or public information campaigns. Analyzes how messages about bodies, risk, care, expertise and/or responsibility are constructed and circulated. Considers how media shape public expectations of patients, professionals and/or institutions. Course content may include real-world examples involving sensitive topics such as illness, disability, gender, sexuality, social class and/or race, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to workforce settings in which effective communication about health is essential, including healthcare industries, public relations, nonprofit outreach, journalism and strategic communication. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in health communication, media studies and public health or policy. Strengthens civic media literacy by examining how health information and misinformation spread through media systems, institutional messaging and cultural narratives. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how portrayals of health are shaped not only by medical knowledge but also by narrative conventions, commercial pressures and/or cultural assumptions. Builds understanding of how media depictions of illness, caregiving and wellness can inform, inspire, mislead and/or stigmatize, depending on framing. Facilitates comparison between professional expertise and popular narratives to better understand how public perceptions of health are formed and challenged. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of medical dramas and documentaries; news coverage of disease outbreaks or medical innovation; health marketing and pharmaceutical advertising; public health campaigns and crisis communication; social media communities around wellness, disability or chronic illness; narratives of caregiving and recovery; depictions of healthcare providers and institutions. May include feminist and/or critical approaches to the intersections of health with topics like gender, race and sexuality. Course material may reference real-world historical and contemporary health controversies when useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Advanced Social Media
prereq_text: Grade of B or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 or JOUR 275/COMM 275 ; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of social media in professional, organizational and/or public communication contexts. Analyzes how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and/or X structure their visibility, engagement and audience expectations. Explores how organizations and individuals craft identity, manage interaction and respond to feedback across different platform cultures. Includes both critical evaluation of existing accounts and hands-on creation of posts, visuals and/or campaigns for specific purposes. Course material may reference real-world social media campaigns related to political, cultural and/or commercial controversy, examined for purposes of communication analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in public relations, branding, journalism, advocacy, content strategy and digital marketing. Builds fluency in platform conventions, analytics, message design and audience targeting; skills applicable in both corporate and nonprofit communication roles. Supports academic growth in media analysis and prepares students for civic participation in increasingly networked communication environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how social media operates not only as a tool for promotion but as a space of negotiation between creators, institutions and publics. Highlights differences between personal posting, strategic messaging and algorithmic influence. Informs reflection on the challenges of authenticity, persuasion and accountability when communication is continuous, participatory and highly public. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of platform affordances and algorithmic logics; branding and identity construction; audience engagement strategies; visual and multimedia storytelling; analytics and performance metrics; influencer models and creator economies; platform policy, moderation and crisis response. Course examples may draw from corporate, political, entertainment, activist and/or nonprofit accounts. Content creation components may involve drafting posts, graphics, videos and/or campaign plans in response to simulated or real-world communication goals. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 or JOUR 275/COMM 275 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: /RELS 480 Religious Communication
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 480/COMM 480 .

subject: COSC
title: Construction Project Planning
prereq_text: COSC 353 ; COSC 375 .
description: Study of construction project planning and scheduling, emphasizing plan reading to identify required activities and sequencing. Students will develop work breakdown structures, define durations and logic relationships and create critical path schedules that span all project phases of a building project from pre-construction through close-out. Using industry-standard software, students will create baselines, update progress, evaluate schedule quality and prepare reporting tools, resulting in working project execution documents. Prerequisite: COSC 353 ; COSC 375 .

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 321 ; junior or senior classification.

Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in DAEN 321 ; junior or senior classification.

prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Human considerations and constraints for data engineering, including human factors of data visualization; data processing and analysis of human physiological, psychological and performance data; the role of human biases in model development, analysis and interpretation; human factors of interactions with machine learning-based artificial intelligence tools in complex systems such as healthcare, manufacturing and transportation. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 .
description: Mathematical optimization algorithms with applications to data analytics; primary topics include convexity, gradient and subgradient methods and their variants, Newton’s and quasi-Newton methods, Frank-Wolfe, duality, derivative-free optimization. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 .

subject: DAEN
title: /ISEN 427 Decision and Risk Analysis
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , DAEN 321 , or STAT 212 .
description: Overview of the state of the art in descriptive and prescriptive theories of decision making under uncertainty with emphasis on the ways in which human decisions depart from normative models of rationality; analytical foundations stemming from several disciplines, economics, psychology, management science; application in engineering systems will be considered. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , DAEN 321 , or STAT 212 . Cross Listing: ISEN 427/DAEN 427 .

subject: DAEN
title: Data Analytics II
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 301 and DAEN 323 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Deep learning, including basic machine learning, supervised learning, logistic regression, loss functions, neural networks, optimization, error back-propagation, regularization and generalization, convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, attention models, applications to natural language processing and computer vision. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in DAEN 301 and DAEN 323 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: DAEN
title: Forecasting Using Machine-Learning Approaches
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 321 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Forecasting principles and methods, including point and interval forecasts; accuracy; statistical methods in the context of forecasting, including exponential smoothing and Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), exogenous variables, seasonality and trends; tree-based models for predictions, prophet models, probabilistic forecasts and predictive and prescriptive analytics. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in DAEN 321 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: DAEN
title: Capstone Senior Design Planning
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 301 ; concurrent enrollment in DAEN 400 , ISEN 427/DAEN 427 , and DAEN 429 .
description: First in a two-course sequence for the capstone senior design experience; formation of a senior design team, visitation with the team sponsor, preparation of the groundwork for the project, preparation of the project charter and collection or acquisition of initial set of data; provision of instructions on different aspects of capstone design, including ethics, design constraints, applicable standards, project management, report writing specifications and requirements, and oral and visual presentations. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in DAEN 301 ; concurrent enrollment in DAEN 400 , ISEN 427/DAEN 427 , and DAEN 429 .

subject: DAEN
title: Capstone Senior Design
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 459 .
description: Second course in a two-course sequence for the capstone senior design experience; continuation of work on the senior design project in teams; data collection, analysis, application of data engineering methods and tools and development of recommendations considering design constraints, evaluation of alternative design, and application of relevant standards; engagement in oral presentations and creation of the project report, with relevant feedback provided during the semester. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in DAEN 459 .

subject: DCED
title: Fundamentals of Pilates
description: Study of Contrology; fundaments of the Pilates Method; mat exercises beginner through advanced; historical background and philosophy; developing modifications of exercises based on individual needs.

subject: DCED
title: Pilates Apparatus I
prereq_text: DCED 205 or approval of instructor.
description: Study of beginner Pilates apparatus work as designed by Joseph H. Pilates; basic principles of Pilates including breathing, pelvic and ribcage placement, scapulae stabilization, head and cervical alignment; uses apparatuses such as reformer, cadillac, chair, and barrel; incorporates the use of props such as rollers, mini balls, physioballs, blocks, therabands and pinky balls into apparatus work. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: DCED 205 or approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Musicality and Movement for Performers
description: Study of music terminology, rhythm, music embodiment, music history, and compositional approaches; exploration of how music, sound, and musicality impact performance; topics include understanding how to communicate with collaborating with musicians and composers; understanding musicality and how it relates to dance practice.

subject: DCED
title: Introduction to Dance Science
prereq_text: Dance science majors or approval of instructor.
description: Introduction to the field of dance science including history, related professions and organizations, post graduate work and current research in the field; exploring basic anatomy and kinesiology concepts relevant to dance; injury prevention, common injuries in dance and return to dance procedures; wellness concepts directly related to dance nutrition, physiological and psychological issues for dancers. Prerequisites: Dance science majors or approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Contact Improvisation
description: Introduction to and exploration of the principles of improvisational partnering including touch, trust, weight sharing, and non-verbal communication; experiment with non-codified/free movement in collaboration with peers including concepts of listening, responding, leading, following, pushing, and pulling; understanding principles of safe alignment and lifting; learning about the history of contact improvisation from creation to present day and understanding the social/cultural influences which shape the form.

subject: DCED
title: Ballet I
prereq_text: Dance science majors, dance concentration majors and dance minors; or approval of instructor.
description: (DANC 1241) Ballet I. Introduction to ballet technique for dancers; series of barre exercises progressing to center work, explanation of positions of the body and port de bras; understand proper body alignment as it relates to ballet technique; appreciation of ballet as an instrument of expression. May be taken 3 times for credit. Prerequisites: Dance science majors, dance concentration majors and dance minors; or approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Movement Lab: Ballet I
prereq_text: Dance science majors; university studies dance concentration majors; dance minors; or approval of instructor.
description: Understand body alignment through ballet technique; assess individual muscular and skeletal imbalances during a ballet technique class; video references of proper body alignment; anatomical explanation and assessment of individual's use of lateral rotation in ballet technique. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: Dance science majors; university studies dance concentration majors; dance minors; or approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Dance Performance Practicum
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.
description: Credit 1. 3 Lab Hours. Dance repertory to engage in dance practice through the process of rehearsals and performance; collaborating in choreographic processes with varying approaches; understanding of rehearsal processes including studio practice, performance spacing, and technical and dress rehearsals; execution of performance in various settings including the stage, community, and other various professional engagements. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Movement Lab: Modern Dance I
prereq_text: Dance Science majors and minors; approval of instructor.
description: Understand body alignment through modern dance; assess individual muscular and skeletal body imbalances during a modern dance class; introduction of how to work with imbalances in the body while executing proper dance technique; understand the structural and muscular alignment of parallel versus lateral rotation. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: Dance Science majors and minors; approval of instructor.

subject: DCED
title: Jazz Dance I
description: Introduction to the study of jazz dance; includes basic steps, locomotor and axial phrases of movement, concepts, and techniques to develop motor and rhythmical skills for jazz movement; development of coordination, stamina, flexibility, and proper alignment; fostering of individual style and creativity towards performing various combinations; historical background and cultural heritage of jazz dance including various styles and choreographers.

subject: DCED
title: Hip Hop Dance I
description: Fundamentals of street dance styles primarily performed to hip hop music or that have evolved as part of hip hop culture; styles may include breaking, locking, and popping; basic steps, concepts, and techniques used to develop motor and rhythmical skills; historical background of the development of hip hop dance and its cultural heritage.

subject: DCED
title: Health Practices for Dancers
prereq_text: Dance science majors only or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
description: Focuses on health issues common to the dancer such as overtraining, drug use and performance anxiety, anatomy in relation to proper dance technique, misalignments, imbalances and injuries common to the dancer. Prerequisites: Dance science majors only or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

description: Data security; cryptography; key exchange; conditional security; unconditional (information-theoretic) security; quantum key distribution; the Kirchhoff-law-Johnson-noise (KLJN) key exchange, electronic noise; advanced issues of KLJN; schemes, protocols, attacks, defense, privacy amplification, credit cards, PUF, autonomous vehicles and smart grids. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 214 ; grade of C or better in ECEN 303 or STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Harnessing Solar Energy: Optics, Photovoltaics and Thermal Systems
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Solar radiation characteristics and measurement; optical coatings including reflection, transmission, absorption and emissivity; concentrating optics, tracking and etendue limit; photovoltaic cells, modules and systems overview; introduction to solar thermal systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Advanced Digital System Design
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 248 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Design, modeling and verification of complex digital systems using hardware description language and electronic system level language. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECEN 248 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Laser Principles and Applications
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Working understanding of the basic principles of laser science, the major components of laser system and their function; examples of laser applications to science, engineering, medicine and industry. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Power Management Circuits and Systems
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 325 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Overview of modern semiconductor power devices, DC-DC linear regulators, switching regulators and battery chargers; emphasis on mathematical foundations, feedback theory, stability and root locus, multi-stage amplifiers, analysis and design of power electronic circuits including DC-DC and AC-DC converters and power supplies; applications on power electronics and power management circuits. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 325 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Microelectronic Device Design
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 325 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.
description: General processes for the fabrication of microelectronic devices and integrated circuits; a review of the electronic properties of semiconductors and carrier transport and recombination; analysis and characterization of p-n junctions, bipolar transistors, and MOS capacitors and transistors; design considerations for achieving optimum performance and practical structures are discussed. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 325 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: VLSI Circuit Design
prereq_text: ECEN 326 .
description: Analysis and design of monolithic analog and digital integrated circuits using NMOS, CMOS and bipolar technologies; device modeling; CAD tools and computer-aided design; design methodologies for LSI and VLSI scale circuits; yield and economics; test and evaluation of integrated circuits. Prerequisite: ECEN 326 .

subject: ECEN
title: Introduction to VLSI Systems Design
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 454 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Introduction to design and fabrication of microelectronic circuits; emphasis on very large scale integration (VLSI) digital systems; use of state-of-the art design methodologies and tools; design of small to medium scale integrated circuits for fabrication. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 454 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Photonics: Fiber and Integrated Optics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Photonics lab including optical power and spectral measurements of singlemode and multimode optical fibers, hands-on arc fusion splicing, lasers, amplifiers, interferometers, photodetectors, integrated optics, fiber-optic devices, optical modulators. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 and ECEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Wireless Communications
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Overview of wireless applications, models for wireless communication channels, modulation formats for wireless communications, multiple access techniques, wireless standards. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: RF and Microwave Wireless Systems
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Introduction to various RF and microwave system parameters, architectures and applications; theory, implementation, and design of RF and microwave systems for communications, radar, sensor, surveillance, navigation, medical and optical applications. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
title: Professional Internship
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 214 or ECEN 248 ; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor and internship agency.
description: 0-1 Lecture Hours. Professional internship in a private company, government agency or laboratory, university or organization to provide work and/or research experience related to the student’s major and career objectives. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 214 or ECEN 248 ; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor and internship agency.

subject: ECON
title: Principles of Economics
description: (ECON 2302) Principles of Economics. Examination of how individuals, firms and governments make choices under scarcity and how their interactions shape markets and economic outcomes; emphasizes opportunity cost, marginal reasoning and the determinants of demand and supply; explores how prices, competition and policy affect efficiency; highlights the value of economic reasoning for understanding real-world behavior and guiding sound policy and decision-making; applications may include causes of market and government failures, labor-market outcomes and strategic behavior in business decision-making; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ECON
title: Poverty, Inequality and Social Policy
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .
description: Analysis of the causes and consequences of poverty and inequality and the role of public policy in shaping economic outcomes; examines the measurement of income, wealth and mobility; explores theoretical and empirical perspectives on market forces, discrimination and opportunity; evaluates the design and impact of social insurance and welfare programs on poverty reduction, incentives and economic performance; emphasizes evidence-based approaches to understanding how policy choices affect efficiency and distributional outcomes in modern economies. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .

subject: ECON
title: Sports Economics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 .
description: Application of microeconomic theory to the business and practice of sports; analyzes market structure, pricing and competition in sports industries; concepts of market power, antitrust policy and valuation of long-term assets; explores strategic behavior using game theory and the effects of imperfect information on decision-making; examines public finance aspects such as stadium subsidies and distributional impacts; emphasizes how sports contexts illustrate broader economic principles and empirical testing of models of behavior. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 .

description: Application of microeconomic theory to the business and practice of sports; analyzes market structure, pricing and competition in sports industries; concepts of market power, antitrust policy and valuation of long-term assets; explores strategic behavior using game theory and the effects of imperfect information on decision-making; examines public finance aspects such as stadium subsidies and distributional impacts; emphasizes how sports contexts illustrate broader economic principles and empirical testing of models of behavior. description: Analysis of the operation and regulation of energy markets and the design of efficient energy policy; applies microeconomic theory and empirical methods to sectors including oil, gasoline, electricity, natural gas, renewables and nuclear power; examines market structure, pricing and investment under evolving technologies and environmental constraints; studies the interaction between energy and environmental policies such as fuel economy standards, carbon pricing and cap-and-trade programs; considers domestic and international experiences to evaluate how regulation and innovation shape energy efficiency, sustainability and market performance. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ECON
title: Environmental Economics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .
description: Application of economic theory to the analysis of global environmental challenges and policy design; examines how market failures and externalities give rise to pollution and resource depletion; evaluates alternative approaches to environmental management including regulation, taxation and market-based instruments such as tradable permits; introduces methods for cost-benefit analysis and non-market valuation of environmental goods. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .

subject: ECON
title: Experimental Economics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .
description: Study of how experiments and behavioral insights advance understanding of economic decision-making; examines deviations from standard models of rationality and self-interest in choices under risk, time and social interaction; introduces experimental methods for testing economic theories and evaluating policy-relevant behavior in laboratory, field and online settings; explores issues of experimental design, data reliability and statistical analysis; emphasizes the development and interpretation of experiments to study individual and group behavior in economics and related fields. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 .

description: Experimental approaches to evaluating economic policies and programs in real-world settings; introduces field experimental methods used to identify causal effects of interventions implemented by firms, governments and NGOs; examines how individuals and organizations respond to changes in incentives across contexts such as education, labor, health, political economy and development; explores the design, implementation and interpretation of randomized evaluations; demonstrates how experimental evidence informs effective and evidence-based policy making in both developed and developing economies. title: Financial Economics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 and ECMT 461 ; or approval of instructor.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: EHRD
title: Instructional Technology and Design
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in EHRD 371 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: This course introduces the design, development and evaluation of technology-enhanced learning experiences in organizational and educational contexts. Emphasis is placed on the application of instructional design models, adult learning principles and emerging tools to create effective and engaging instructional materials. Students will examine the role of instructional technology within the design process, evaluate learning platforms and authoring tools and produce digital learning content using accessible software. The course also explores current trends shaping instructional technology practice in the field of human resource development. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 371 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: 21st-Century Literature and Culture
description: Introduction to some of the major literary and cultural forms of the twenty-first century. Course topics might include texts from a variety of national and cultural origins, different approaches to a relevant topic or representations of contemporary historical events. subject: ENGL
title: Human Thinking and Digital Culture
description: Introduction to digital culture(s); exposure to some methodologies for the interpretation and critique of digital media from the humanities. These may include but are not limited to approaches from critical data studies, media studies, digital humanities, and the history of science and technology. Students can expect to gain experience analyzing digital media and expect to develop critical thinking and intercultural competence while engaging in respectful discourse on complex topics related to digital cultures. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

subject: ENGR
title: Interdisciplinary Design
prereq_text: Senior classification and approval of instructor.
description: Instruction and practice in the design process applied to an interdisciplinary design project including establish the customer need; determine requirements in terms of function (what) and performance (how well); develop alternative design concepts; perform trade-off studies among performance, cost and schedule; embodiment and detail design; iterate the above steps; major interdisciplinary design project. Prerequisites: Senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: ENGR
title: Interdisciplinary Design II
prereq_text: ENGR 401 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Product detail and design development process including case studies; may include project management, marketing considerations, manufacturing detailed design specifications; failure modes, applications of codes and standards, selection of design margins; product (component) development guidelines; intellectual property, product liability and ethical responsibility. Prerequisites: ENGR 401 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ENGR
title: Global Engineering Design
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Intercultural models and their application to engineering design in diverse, multinational and multidisciplinary settings; engineering design project working in international teams of students, faculty and industry experts; applying engineering skills to the project; includes the study and application of intercultural models, global enterprise fundamentals and remote collaboration technologies; required for the International Engineering Certificate. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Field Entomology in the Tropics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 ; or approval of instructor; any course in entomology recommended.
description: A field-based course conducted in Costa Rica at the Texas A&M Soltis Center for Research and Education that examines the diversity, behavior and natural history of tropical insects. Emphasis is placed on collecting insects, specimen preparation and identification, behavioral observation and experimental research, along with the development of skills in field note-keeping, teamwork and scientific communication. The course provides direct experience with tropical ecosystems and addresses the challenges associated with studying and conserving biodiversity. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 ; or approval of instructor; any course in entomology recommended.

title: Electronics Testing II
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ESET 349 and ESET 352 ; junior or senior classification in electronic systems engineering technology.

Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ESET 352 ; junior or senior classification in electronic systems engineering technology.

title: Media Industries
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. Examples may draw on current and historical cases across major and emerging sectors. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 345 and JOUR 345 .

title: /PHIL 376 Philosophy, Film and Evil
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students examine the concept of evil through the medium of film, exploring how cinema reflects, interprets and interrogates philosophical understandings of morality, suffering and human nature. Students engage with major philosophical approaches to evil, such as classical theodicies and free will defenses and modern accounts of cruelty, moral psychology and systemic violence, while analyzing cinematic depictions that illuminate these themes. Students investigate how film both represents and questions moral experience. Lectures, discussions, screenings and writing projects combine to cultivate philosophical insight through visual storytelling in cinema. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware discourse on contentious issues and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they are able to competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. subject: FINC
title: Applied Investment Analysis
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Theoretical and analytical developments in security and strategy selection in portfolio management with an emphasis on absolute returns and from the perspective of a hedge fund manager; includes macroeconomic analysis and portfolio performance evaluation; concepts applied to the allocation of investments in one or more student-managed portfolios. subject: FIVS
title: Forensic Molecular Biology
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in FIVS 308 ; FIVS-SCE majors.
description: This course is designed to illustrate the use of a variety of molecular biology methods for forensic applications. The core elements that will be covered include prokaryotic and eukaryotic genome structure and function; interrelationship of DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis; transcription, translation, replication; gene expression and regulation; recombinant DNA techniques; PCR; and DNA sequencing. Students will gain an appreciation and understanding of the underlying molecular biology techniques that are used in a diverse array of settings, including blood analysis, blood typing, DNA fingerprinting and genetic testing. The potential future use of advanced sequencing technologies for forensic and other applications will be discussed. Additionally, the social, ethical and legal implications of these procedures and applications will be fully considered. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in FIVS 308 ; FIVS-SCE majors.

subject: GENE
title: /BIMS 320 Biomedical Genetics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Study of modern genetics with an emphasis on biomedical and health-related applications of the mammalian genome. Topics include classical Mendelian inheritance, pedigree and genetic risk analysis, population genetics, quantitative genetics and the molecular basis of gene structure and function, including DNA replication, transcription, mutation and gene regulation. The course examines how genetic variation and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to disease and phenotypic diversity, and introduces advanced concepts in cytogenetics, epigenetics, cancer genetics and genomics. Contemporary applications such as genome sequencing, gene therapy, personalized medicine and associated ethical considerations are also addressed. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 315, GENE-320 or BIMS-320. title: Geography of the United States
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: This systematic and regional course introduces geographic issues covering the geography of the United States from environmental, political, social/cultural and economic perspectives with a focus on the many ways that culture, politics, economics and social difference are manifested in and through spatial relations and processes. Our case studies will emphasize that the United States is an ever-changing configuration of ideas, institutions, people and objects. This course also aims to develop conceptual tools for critical thinking, rather than an encyclopedic knowledge of the United States’ geographic features. Finally, the course introduces students to a variety of concepts and methods that geographers use to analyze spatial patterns and processes. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: GEOG
title: Environmental Justice
prereq_text: GEOG 201 or GEOG 202 ; junior or senior classification.
description: This course examines the uneven distribution of environmental benefits and burdens across society, drawing on the scholarly literature referred to as environmental justice research. You will examine historical and contemporary evidence for disparities in exposure to environmental hazards, including but not limited to air and water pollution, as well as disparities in access to environmental amenities, including but not limited to urban greenspace. Topics address variation in environmental conditions and policy outcomes across different demographic and geographic contexts, including those associated with race, gender, ethnicity and class, as these social categories are used in empirical research and policy analysis. The course treats these social categories as analytical descriptors rather than normative or ideological claims. Content includes controversial and contested scholarly perspectives on environmental issues, reflecting multiple explanatory frameworks for understanding the causes of and proposed policy responses to uneven environmental distributions. Drawing on readings from a range of disciplines, such as environmental science, geography and urban planning, you will evaluate proposed explanations for observed patterns, including but not limited to market dynamics, land-use decisions, regulatory enforcement, historical settlement patterns and institutional decision-making processes. You will also compare policy and governance responses discussed in the scholarly literature, such as market-based mechanisms, participatory decision-making arrangements and strengthened regulatory oversight, assessing their assumptions, empirical support and trade-offs. The course emphasizes evidence-based reasoning and civil discourse, preparing you to engage constructively with contentious environmental policy contexts. An independent research project will train you to develop and defend an analytical argument related to an environmental justice issue of your choosing using appropriate evidence. Throughout the course, your work will be evaluated on the quality of analysis and reasoning, not on agreement with any particular political, moral or ideological position. Prerequisites: GEOG 201 or GEOG 202 ; junior or senior classification.

Native North American history from earliest habitation to the present; addresses widely varying Indigenous groups; themes include but are not limited to cultural exchange, colonial conflict, U.S. Indian policy, resistance and revitalization, sovereignty and self-determination, activism. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Also taught at Qatar campus.

subject: HORT
title: Professions in Horticulture
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Comprehensive view of the opportunities in the science, technology and art of horticultural sciences and potential career paths; sub-disciplines by crop (fruit, vegetable, viticulture, nut, ornamental crops, floral crops, controlled environment and urban horticulture) and approach (research, technology, biotechnology, mechanization, genetics, genomics, and breeding, phenomics, landscaping, production, sustainability, floral design, indoor farming, and entrepreneurship); examination of the national and international scope and economic, environmental and health impacts of horticulture; major horticultural regions in Texas; interactions with representatives and leaders of various horticultural industries; featured horticulture innovations presented by inventors; development of an online professional profile, such as LinkedIn.

subject: HORT
title: Trees and Shrubs for Sustainable Built Environments
prereq_text: BIOL 101 , BIOL 111 , BIOL 113 , HORT 301 , LAND 101 , ECCB 205 , grade of C or better in HORT 201 , or approval of instructor.
description: Better known woody ornamental trees and shrubs; identification, morphology, classification, nomenclature and adaptability for use in landscape environments. subject: HORT
title: Plants for Sustainable Landscapes
prereq_text: BIOL 101 , BIOL 111 , BIOL 113 , HORT 301 , LAND 101 , ECCB 205 , grade of C or better in HORT 201 , or approval of instructor.
description: Identification and use of indigenous and introduced landscape plants; plants for special uses in urban environments; emphasis on plants' ornamental attributes, cultural requirements, and adaptability in urban and suburban environments. title: Introduction to Plant Physiology
prereq_text: BIOL 101 , BIOL 111 or BIOL 113 and CHEM 222 or CHEM 227 .
description: Study of principal life processes of higher plants; influence of environmental factors on these processes; agricultural and ecological significance of life processes of plants. Prerequisite: BIOL 101 , BIOL 111 or BIOL 113 and CHEM 222 or CHEM 227 .

subject: HORT
title: Issues in Horticulture
prereq_text: HORT 202 ; grade of C or better in HORT 201 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Analysis and exploration of factors that impinge on modern horticultural systems, including technological, environmental, economic and societal issues; emphasis on student-driven research on critical issues that affect a horticultural industry sector of interest to the student. Self-driven research is coupled with writing-intensive coursework. Prerequisites: HORT 202 ; grade of C or better in HORT 201 ; junior or senior classification.

description: Continuation of IDIS 443 ; second-semester in capstone design sequence; design and development of a solution(s) to a distribution problem using systematic research methods and tools in a team-based environment; application of a systems-thinking approach for the development of best practices related to the chosen field such as logistics, operations, sales, etc. to determine the impact of their proposed solution on other component areas of the business. title: Foundations of Education - Community, Values and Civics
description: This course is intended to provide prospective teachers, and all undergraduate majors, with background information and insight to explore the historical, philosophical and societal foundations of education for all students. subject: INTA
title: Cyberpolicy
prereq_text: INTS and INTA majors; junior or senior classification.
description: Exploration of the intersection of technology, policy, strategy and national security, focusing on the national security implications of cyberspace and cyber-enabled technologies, including cyber-enabled influence operations, in support of national security interests. It is not a technical course, but will provide the background necessary for students to understand, discuss and analyze relevant issues related to cyberspace and cyber-enabled operations and activities. The course will also introduce and examine the cyberspace aspects of a number of disruptive technologies in a national security context, including artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous weapons systems, biotechnology and others. Prerequisites: INTS and INTA majors; junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: American Mass Media
description: (COMM 1307) American Mass Media. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the development and role of mass media in the United States across print, broadcast and digital platforms. Surveys ways journalism, entertainment, advertising and/or social media industries have evolved alongside major legal, economic and technological changes. Examines how media shape public understanding of news, culture and community life. Course content may reference current events or contested media topics for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy essential for participation in contemporary information environments. Supports workforce preparation for fields involving communication, marketing, journalism, public relations, policy and content creation. Strengthens ability to interpret media systems and evaluate messages. Provides academic grounding for further study in media, communication and related social sciences, while promoting informed engagement with public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways media messages are not neutral transmissions of facts or entertainment, but are reflections of institutional structures, economic incentives and cultural values. Clarifies differences between news, opinion, analysis, persuasion and/or misinformation, enabling critical comparison. Considers responsible media as involving critical interpretation, evidence assessment and awareness of perspective. Applies media literacy concepts to support informed citizenry through an understanding of First Amendment protections. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media history and industry development; journalism and press freedom; advertising and entertainment business models; media law and ethics; corporate ownership and consolidation; social media platforms and audience participation; representation in film, television and news; and the role of media in elections, crisis coverage or cultural debate. Course materials may include real-world examples that involve political and/or social controversy, examined for purposes of understanding the role of media in the United States and around the globe.

subject: JOUR
title: Mass Media Information
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 ; freshman or sophomore classification; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores methods for locating, verifying and organizing information for use in journalism and related media fields. Examines how reporters, researchers and content creators identify credible sources, interpret data and manage competing forms of evidence. Covers procedures for working with public records, interviews, documents and digital databases. Introduces basic interview techniques and requires a range of interviews. Addresses legal and ethical standards guiding information access, attribution and responsible use. May reference real-world news events and/or disputed claims for purposes of evaluating information practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in journalism, public communication, strategic media, research and content production where accuracy and credibility are essential. Builds fluency in information gathering and source evaluation for professional settings such as newsrooms, nonprofit advocacy, policy communication and organizational messaging. Supports academic preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, media law, research methods or data journalism. Strengthens civic readiness by reinforcing principles of evidence-based decision-making in public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how information is not merely “found” but actively selected, framed and interpreted through methodological choices. Highlights differences between rumor, opinion and verifiable fact, while showing how even credible sources may present information with limitations or bias. Considers that responsible information gathering requires transparency in process as much as accuracy in outcome. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include source credibility and verification; interviewing and data collection methods; public records and open-source intelligence; fact-checking and revision protocols; digital search strategies; statistical interpretation and data visualization; legal frameworks governing access and privacy including public records legislation at the federal and state levels; ethical considerations in handling sensitive or incomplete information. May draw on journalism, government documents, nonprofit reports or corporate communications when relevant to understanding differences in information intent and reliability. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 ; freshman or sophomore classification; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

subject: JOUR
title: Media Writing I
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 and JOUR 200 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
description: (COMM 2311) Media Writing I. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores foundational practices of news and media writing across print, digital and broadcast formats. Covers core principles of reporting, source development, interviewing, story structure, clarity, accuracy and ethics. Emphasizes deadline writing and editorial standards such as Associated Press style. Includes both classroom instruction and lab-based field reporting and/or writing practice. Course content may reference current events or public controversies as real-time reporting contexts, examined for purposes of journalistic analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds competencies essential for careers in journalism, public communication, media production and content strategy, including information gathering, source evaluation, editing and professional writing. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, multimedia storytelling, strategic communication or public affairs. Provides transferable skills for civic participation by strengthening the ability to assess evidence, verify claims and communicate clearly in public-facing formats. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the difference between everyday writing and journalistic writing defined by professional standards of fairness, attribution, style and verification. Considers that responsible reporting involves interpretation, fact assessment, and acknowledgment of perspective without slant or speculation. Develops recognition of how word choice, structure and sourcing shape public understanding. Analyzes how news stories serve both individuals and communities. Develops understanding of professional ethics standards. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news values, interviewing techniques, attribution and quoting, hard news and feature formats, multimedia writing, legal constraints and ethical dilemmas in reporting. Exercises may involve real or hypothetical scenarios involving crime, politics, social issues or public institutions, used solely to develop reporting judgment and writing skills. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 and JOUR 200 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

subject: JOUR
title: Television Sports Production
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how televised sports are produced behind the scenes, from planning to live execution. Introduces the roles of producers, directors, announcers, camera operators and technical crews, emphasizing collaboration across production teams. Examines historic developments in sports broadcasting alongside contemporary industry practices, including graphics, replay operations and/or real-time storytelling. Course content may reference high-pressure or emotionally charged broadcast situations for the purpose of professional analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops workforce-ready skills in research, coordination and deadline-driven collaboration through engagement with live event production and sports media workflows. Provides practical experience in broadcast storytelling, technical setup and real-time decision-making. Builds foundations for effective communication under pressure, rapid problem-solving and teamwork, competencies that transfer to careers in media, athletics, production management and other professional or academic settings requiring precision and adaptability. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports broadcasting functions as both entertainment and institutional messaging, shaping narratives of competition, identity and community. Examines ways production choices, such as camera angles, commentary, graphics and pacing, frame audience perception. Informs reflection on how spectacle, emotion and/or technology intersect in mediated sport. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of broadcast history and industry structure; producer and director decision-making; live graphics and replay systems; commentary and on-air performance roles; camera work and technical operations; crisis management during live events; ethics of representation in sports storytelling; evolution of streaming, social media integration and fan engagement. Course materials may include footage depicting intense competition, injury or heightened emotion, examined for purposes of professional critique.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 215 Interviewing - Principles and Practice
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of interviewing as a purposeful form of interpersonal communication. Focus on questioning strategies, listening and interaction between the interviewer and interviewee. Examines informative, persuasive, survey and/or employment interview contexts. Develops skills as both the interviewer and the interviewee. Emphasizes how structure, audience, goals and setting shape communication choices. Addresses the logical and psychological bases of interviewing. Class applications may involve exposure to perspectives and experiences across social, cultural and professional backgrounds. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds transferable skills essential to journalism, media, public communication and organizational practice. Involves questioning, listening, adaptation to audience and purpose and interaction across varied goals. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 250 New Media and the Independent Voice
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of new and independent media in shaping cultural, political and social life. Surveys forms such as blogs, podcasts, video, digital storytelling and social media platforms. Considers how independent voices create, challenge and reshape narratives in communities and public discourse. Attention to the relationship between personal voice, creativity and professional practice, as well as to issues of credibility, trust, ethics and representation. Explores how traditional and independent media engage with topics including activism, identity, politics and/or popular culture, highlighting both opportunities and challenges for communication in digital environments as they are constantly evolving. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy and production skills relevant to journalism, communication, marketing and/or creative industries. Develops competence in analyzing the credibility, reach and influence of independent media. Strengthens preparation for roles requiring digital fluency, critical thinking and the ability to adapt messages across platforms. Provides tools for both professional communication and civic engagement in a media environment shaped by independent voices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how independent media can be both a space of empowerment and a site of contestation. Highlights how digital platforms amplify personal, cultural and political voices, while also raising ethical and practical challenges. Highlights how identity, power and representation shape media production and reception. Develops understanding of the opportunities and limits of independent communication in contemporary society. Explores the opportunities and challenges presented by changes in the media landscape. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of blogs, podcasts, video and social media platforms; exploration of digital storytelling and creative expression; consideration of ethics, representation and credibility in independent media; analysis of activism, politics and identity as expressed through digital platforms; evaluation of how independent voices influence communities, industries and public life. Course applications may draw on popular culture, current events and emerging issues. Discussions may also engage with controversial or contested topics, reflecting the role of independent media in addressing subjects that shape public dialogue. Cross Listing: COMM 250/JOUR 250 .

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Involves skills relevant to designing messages, engaging audiences and producing or analyzing digital media across professional platforms. Prepares for advanced academic study in communication, media studies, journalism and related fields where digital fluency and critical media analysis are expected. Promotes awareness of how traditional media and independent media practices can contribute to civic discourse, cultural participation and emerging communication markets. Encourages media literacy in both communication careers and everyday life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how new media platforms differ from legacy communication systems in structure, purpose and power. Highlights the role of individual voice, audience interaction and platform design in shaping meaning and influence. Encourages recognition that public communication through digital media may challenge assumptions about authority, expertise and representation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis or creation of blogs, podcasts, social media campaigns, digital storytelling or multimedia commentary; exploration of how mass media engage politics, identity, culture and public issues; study of persuasion, narrative, audience engagement and message strategy in digital contexts. Assignments may involve analysis, production or both, depending on the instructor’s approach. Course materials may involve perspectives or content reflecting varied experiences, beliefs and interpretations encountered in contemporary media environments. Cross Listing: COMM 255/JOUR 255 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 275 Introduction to Social Media
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores social media as a communication environment shaped by technology, audience, participation and platform design. Surveys major platforms, concepts and theories used to understand how individuals, organizations and communities create, share and interpret digital content. Examines how social media intersects with journalism, marketing, activism, entertainment and/or everyday communication. Considers how digital communication practices reflect and influence public discourse, society and culture. Engagement with real-world examples may involve topics connected to politics, religion, identity, ethics and/or lived experiences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices connected to media industries, strategic messaging, journalism, advertising, nonprofit work, politics and other forms of public communication. Involves skills relevant to content creation, audience analysis, audience engagement, platform analysis and communication strategy. Connects to professional and academic paths in media, communication, journalism, marketing, public affairs and digital culture. Supports academic preparation to analyze ways social media shapes institutional messaging, cultural participation, community formation and civic dialogue. Develops applied skill in using social media strategically within entrepreneurial, organizational or community campaign contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication via social media platforms differs from legacy media in participation, access and influence. Explores communication theories and strategies underpinning social media communication. Highlights tensions involving credibility, persuasion, privacy, visibility and/or identity in digital environments. Builds understanding of how platforms shape perception, behavior and communication norms in ways that are not always immediately visible. Supports informed assessment of one’s own media usage patterns and communication practices as case material for analysis. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication theories, platform histories and digital ecosystems; analysis of messaging strategies and audience behavior; consideration of digital identity, participation and online communities; exploration of ethics, credibility, privacy, representation and influence in online environments; examination of how platforms shape visibility, participation and public discourse; study of consent, branding, advocacy, journalism and influencer practices; comparison of interactive and traditional media. Course materials may reflect varied perspectives and examples from professional, cross-cultural and/or global contexts. Cross Listing: COMM 275/JOUR 275 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 307 Communication Law and Policy
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the legal and ethical foundations of communication in journalism, media and public life. Considers First Amendment principles, constitutional protections and limits on free speech and free press. Surveys key areas of communication law, including libel, privacy, copyright, obscenity, advertising, broadcast regulation and/or digital communication. Considers ethical standards and professional responsibilities that shape communication practices across diverse contexts. Directs attention to the tensions between individual expression, institutional regulation and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in understanding how legal frameworks and ethical codes guide communication decisions in professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds skills for identifying risks, evaluating responsibilities and applying standards to journalism, media and/or organizational settings. Provides preparation for careers requiring knowledge of communication law, professional ethics and public accountability. Strengthens civic awareness by highlighting the role of free expression in democracy and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about “free speech” and “freedom of the press” differ from their legal and professional realities. Encourages awareness of the limits, protections and obligations that accompany communication rights. Expands understanding of how legal rules intersect with ethical reasoning, professional standards and social expectations. Promotes careful reflection on how controversies over speech, press and media practice reveal broader tensions in democratic societies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of First Amendment foundations and constitutional principles; libel, privacy and copyright; obscenity, advertising and broadcast regulation; law and policy for digital and social media; ethical theories and professional codes; accountability, fairness, diversity and harm in communication practice. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of legal and ethical analysis within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: COMM 307/JOUR 301 .

Builds skills for identifying risks, evaluating responsibilities and applying standards to journalism, media and/or organizational settings. Provides preparation for careers requiring knowledge of communication law, professional ethics and public accountability. Strengthens civic awareness by highlighting the role of free expression in democracy and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about “free speech” and “freedom of the press” differ from their legal and professional realities. Encourages awareness of the limits, protections and obligations that accompany communication rights. Expands understanding of how legal rules intersect with ethical reasoning, professional standards and social expectations. Promotes careful reflection on how controversies over speech, press and media practice reveal broader tensions in democratic societies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of First Amendment foundations and constitutional principles; libel, privacy and copyright; obscenity, advertising and broadcast regulation; law and policy for digital and social media; ethical theories and professional codes; accountability, fairness, diversity and harm in communication practice. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of legal and ethical analysis within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: COMM 307/JOUR 301 .

subject: JOUR
title: The Mass Media and Politics
prereq_text: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements. Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 302 and POLS 302 .

subject: JOUR
title: Media Writing II
prereq_text: JOUR 203 , enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Builds on foundational practices of news and media writing by shifting from structured exercises to more independent, publication-oriented work. Deepens proficiency in interviewing, sourcing, verification and AP style while introducing longer-form formats such as features, profiles, explanatory reporting and/or issue-driven narratives. Applies legal and ethical frameworks through scenario-based decision-making rather than rule recall. Reinforces core reporting habits of verification, accuracy and clarity, while advancing professional editorial readiness. May draw on current events or public controversies, addressed through journalistic standards of accuracy, attribution and fairness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides practical experience valued in newsrooms, digital media, public affairs, nonprofit communications and content development roles requiring rapid research and fact-based writing. Strengthens transferable skills in information gathering, synthesis and public accountability, useful in academic and civic contexts where claims and sources must be critically evaluated. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how journalistic authority is earned through transparency, corroboration and structural discipline rather than voice alone. Builds awareness of framing choices — what to include, exclude or emphasize — and how these decisions influence audience interpretation. Examines reporting not only as information transfer but as ongoing negotiation between accuracy, access, ethics and presentation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include advanced interviewing techniques; background research and source vetting; feature and profile writing; beat development; editorial rewriting and collaborative critique; application of media law to reporting dilemmas; corrections and accountability practices; integration of photographs, headlines or multimedia assets based on publication constraints. May involve field reporting on campus or community issues, conducted within ethical and professional guidelines. Prerequisites: JOUR 203 , enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
