subject: JOUR
title: Editing for the Mass Media
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles and practices of editing across print, broadcast and digital media, focusing on journalistic style and structure. Covers sentence-level refinement, fact-checking, clarity and consistency review, correction of grammatical and structural errors and adaptation of content for varied platforms and audiences. Emphasizes editorial judgment in tightening text without distorting voice or meaning. Includes headline and subhead writing, style guide application, peer-editing and awareness of how legal and ethical standards apply to editing decisions rather than reporting alone. Builds on media writing coursework by shifting focus from content creation to evaluation, revision and publication-readiness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds advanced competencies central to newsroom, publishing, marketing and content strategy roles, including copyediting, information verification, editorial collaboration and style precision. Reinforces habits essential to academic and professional writing in fields where clarity, accuracy and/or credibility are required. Supports civic literacy by strengthening the ability to assess how wording, structure and omission influence public interpretation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how editing is not merely correction but interpretation, requiring awareness of audience, tone and implication. Considers how editorial choices shape storytelling, accessibility and fairness as much as writing choices do. Builds recognition of how cultural context, legal obligation and ethical norms factor into seemingly small changes. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include editing for grammar, structure and flow; fact-checking and error detection; AP style and style guide adaptation; headline and SEO writing; tone and audience calibration; legal and ethical considerations in revision; collaborative workflows between writers and editors; and analysis of published examples from news, nonprofit and commercial media. Exercises may draw from real or simulated stories involving sensitive or controversial subject matter, introduced for building skills at accurate and responsible editing practice. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director; junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: Photojournalism I
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores still photography practices in journalistic contexts, focusing on camera operation, composition, ethical standards and field-based image production. Emphasizes photography as a tool for documenting people, places, events and/or everyday life. Assignments simulate real-world photojournalism through location-based shoots, peer critique and portfolio development. Course content may involve exposure to newsworthy situations, including moments of conflict, hardship and/or public emotion, examined for the purpose of understanding practices of visual documentation and evaluating ethical and communicative impacts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies essential for careers in journalism, visual media, public relations, marketing and content creation, including technical literacy, deadline management, ethical decision-making and client/audience awareness. Supports preparation for advanced visual storytelling, multimedia reporting and professional communication roles requiring accuracy, clarity and visual credibility. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how photographic choices such as framing, timing, proximity and editing can shape meaning as much as subject matter. Considers how journalistic imagery involves artistic judgment, public responsibility and industry codes of ethics. Builds awareness of how images circulate, persuade and/or inform differently across media platforms. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news, feature, portrait, sports and event photography; composition, lighting and image sequencing; ethics of representation, consent and vulnerable subjects; history of visual journalism and iconic images; storytelling across single images and multi-photo narratives. Coursework may involve documenting diverse communities or public environments, approached with sensitivity to accuracy, fairness and professional standards. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 317 Social Media Law
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Laws and regulations applied to social media, including communication law applied to enduring issues in the social media context; legal problems unique to social media; free speech, commercial speech and employment law as they affect individual users of social media as well as groups and organizations promoting points of view or products via social media, and employers. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 317/JOUR 317 .

subject: JOUR
title: Visual Journalism
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the analysis and creation of visual communication in journalistic and documentary contexts. Examines how photographs, illustrations, layout, color and digital design shape meaning across platforms such as news, magazines, social feeds and long-form multimedia projects. Traces aesthetic, technological and ethical developments in visual journalism while incorporating hands-on work in photography, design and digital illustration. Course content may involve exposure to controversial news imagery, including depictions of conflict, crisis and/or intense public emotion, for the purpose of developing visual judgment, ethical decision-making and critical analysis of journalistic documentation. Course content may also review editorial illustrations connected to opinion stories involving politics and/or cultural topics to develop an understanding of the impact of visual communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies needed in media professions where visual literacy, editing and/or content production are central. Supports preparation for careers in journalism, documentary work, publishing, advertising and digital communication by emphasizing visual judgment, technical execution and ethical decision-making. Strengthens academic pathways in media studies and provides transferable skills for civic participation in a visually driven information environment. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how images can inform, persuade and/or mislead depending on composition, context and display. Highlights the interpretive layers behind seemingly objective visuals, including choices of framing, editing, sequencing and captioning. Informs reflections on ways visual representation can intersect with questions of identity, credibility and public memory. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of photojournalism and reportage; layout and design principles; illustration and editorial graphics; data visualization and infographics; historical shifts in visual journalism; ethical and legal questions surrounding image use; and the influence of social media platforms on visual circulation. Creative components may involve curated image essays, design mockups or original photographic assignments completed within professional guidelines. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Mobile Journalism
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores multimedia reporting using mobile devices as primary tools for journalistic production. Covers techniques in audio gathering, digital still photography and video documentation, with emphasis on recording, editing, scripting and real-time publishing across multiple digital platforms. Simulates newsroom environments through deadline-based production, critique and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds core competencies required in contemporary newsrooms and digital media industries, including rapid field reporting, technical versatility, editorial collaboration and/or content adaptation across platforms. Supports workforce preparation in journalism, strategic communication, digital content creation, nonprofit storytelling and public information roles. Reinforces transferable skills, including judgment under pressure, visual literacy and evidence-based storytelling, relevant to civic participation and public-facing professions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the distinction between casual mobile content creation and journalistic media production grounded in ethics, verification and clarity of purpose. Encourages critical reflection on how choices in framing, sequencing and platform affect audience interpretation. Demonstrates how professional credibility is constructed through transparency, accuracy and responsibility in visual storytelling. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of field recording techniques; audio scripting and narration; photo composition and ethical editing; video sequencing and interview setups; platform-specific publishing strategies; story pitching and editorial feedback; coverage of unfolding public events; ethical judgment and/or professional analysis. Assignments may involve documenting real-world environments — including emotionally charged settings or moments of conflict, controversy, hardship, celebration or vulnerability — approached for the purposes of visual analysis and responsible reporting. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Reporting Sports
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of sports reporting across professional, collegiate and community contexts. Covers live event reporting, interviewing, beat reporting, deadline writing and industry-standard formatting such as AP style. Emphasizes ethical judgment in reporting of competition, emotion and/or controversy, while maintaining neutrality, accuracy and professionalism. Simulates newsroom workflows through field reporting, editorial review and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds applied competencies essential to careers in journalism, broadcasting, media relations, sports communication and content production. Reinforces transferable skills such as rapid information synthesis, audience adaptation, collaborative communication and deadline management. Supports broader workforce preparation in fields that require precise coordination, public-facing documentation and/or real-time decision-making. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how sports journalism blends entertainment, data, human interest and public accountability. Highlights the role of the journalist in navigating fandom, institutional access and representation, balancing narrative engagement with accuracy and fairness. Encourages awareness of how reporting choices influence perceptions of competition, identity and/or community. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include field interviewing; live coverage of sporting events; beat development; game recaps and feature storytelling; multimedia integration (audio, photo, mobile journalism); sports ethics and conflict-of-interest management; representation of athletes and teams across gender, race, class or institutional lines. Course material may involve observation or documentation of competitive, emotional and/or contentious sports environments, approached with sensitivity and professional responsibility. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 365 International Communication
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; COMM-365 also taught at Qatar campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts, theories and practices in international communication and global journalism. Examines comparative media systems by analyzing how media develops across different political, cultural and economic contexts. Considers how world news circulates: who produces it, how it travels and how it is interpreted by diverse audiences. Examines issues such as freedom of the press, political propaganda, international advertising, public diplomacy and/or the impact of digital technologies. Students engage with theoretical, pragmatic, political and/or ethical perspectives to analyze how power, culture and/or technology shape global information exchange. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools for working with global media across cultural differences. Builds skills in evaluating international news, identifying propaganda and disinformation and applying ethical standards across cultures. Prepares students for careers in journalism, public affairs and related fields requiring cross-cultural awareness and media literacy. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Develops understandings of press freedom, news values and global information flows, recognizing that media systems operate within distinct political, cultural and economic contexts; exploring how interconnected stories affecting different countries and regions have developed through globalization and social media. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of comparative media systems; study of world news flows and international reporting; press freedom, censorship and ethics; political propaganda, public diplomacy and soft power; international advertising and global news cultures; impact of digital technologies, social media and generative AI; challenges of disinformation and “fake news” in global communication. Course materials may include discussion of sensitive or controversial topics, presented from multiple perspectives to reflect the diversity of global media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; COMM-365 also taught at Qatar campus. Cross Listing: COMM 365/JOUR 365 .

subject: JOUR
title: Political Reporting
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced reporting and writing skills through coverage of political actors, campaigns, institutions, policies and/or public debate. Emphasizes journalistic forms such as straight news, analysis, commentary, deadline reporting and/or long-form enterprise work. Coursework may involve interviewing public officials and stakeholders, sourcing public records, verifying factual claims and writing for publication under real-world time constraints. Engages legal and ethical challenges common to political reporting through case-based analysis and professional decision-making. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Prepares students for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, political campaign messaging and media production requiring accuracy, fairness and accountability in public-facing work. Reinforces transferable skills in source evaluation, poll evaluation, fact assessment, editorial judgment and deadline coordination. Supports media literacy and civic readiness by strengthening the ability to interpret competing claims and document political developments with clarity and restraint. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how journalistic credibility is constructed through sourcing, structure, transparency and consistency with professional standards. Highlights how political information circulates across formats such as news stories, speeches, commentary, newsletters, podcasts and/or social media. Encourages attention to how misinformation, framing or selective emphasis influence interpretation, requiring constant assessment of reliability and relevance. Explores ethical and legal issues regarding public records laws and the First Amendment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of interviewing, source development, fact-checking, news and feature structure, commentary and analysis writing, polling interpretation, deadline reporting and long-form enterprise work; consideration of media ethics, transparency, fairness and public accountability in coverage of elections, legislation, policy debates and/or political conflict. Course material may involve disputed events, competing narratives or controversial figures engaged for purposes of journalistic evaluation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Arts and Entertainment Journalism
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores reporting and writing practices specific to arts and entertainment journalism across genres such as film, music, visual arts, live performance, food and/or popular culture. Emphasizes feature writing, criticism and commentary, combining descriptive narrative with analytical evaluation. Includes regular drafting, revision and editorial feedback in workshop-style settings. Course material may reference real-world works or events that evoke strong personal and/or cultural responses; such content is approached through ethical journalistic standards of observation, fairness and critique. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops professional habits in research, interviewing, deadline writing and editorial collaboration relevant to journalism, reviewing, cultural reporting, media production, public relations and arts programming. Supports academic pathways in media criticism, narrative nonfiction and cultural studies. Reinforces transferable skills in analytical writing, public communication and civic engagement through responsible evaluation of cultural expression. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how arts and entertainment coverage blends storytelling with informed judgment, requiring both subject knowledge and ethical standards. Informs consideration of how tone, evidence and perspective shape credibility in evaluative writing. Explores how cultural journalism influences public conversation not by prescribing taste, but by modeling interpretation, context and reflection. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and practice of feature profiles, reviews, cultural commentary and long-form narrative; genre-specific approaches to writing about art, food, music, theater, fashion, television and film; techniques for descriptive reporting and sensory detail; methods of comparative evaluation; ethics of criticism and representation. Course content may involve engagement with controversial works, sensitive subject matter or emotionally charged performances, addressed for purposes of journalistic analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Business Reporting
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of covering business, finance and the economy for general audiences. Emphasizes how companies, markets, government policy and consumer behavior intersect to shape everyday life. Trains students to locate, interpret and translate information from sources such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, economic datasets, industry reports and executive interviews. Coursework may draw on real-world developments involving corporate strategy, labor trends, inflation, energy, technology or regional economic change. Topics are approached through journalistic standards of accuracy, clarity and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for careers in business journalism, data reporting, financial communications, public information and strategic media roles. Develops transferable skills in document interpretation, interviewing, trend analysis and deadline storytelling that apply across sectors including government, nonprofit, policy and corporate communication. Supports academic advancement in media studies, economics, public policy or analytics by reinforcing evidence-based reasoning and clear explanatory writing. Strengthens civic readiness by improving understanding of how economic decisions are communicated to the public and in turn affected by public response. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how business reporting is not limited to stock prices or balance sheets but involves explaining systems, including how decisions made by corporations, policymakers and markets influence employment, cost of living, infrastructure and opportunity. Informs consideration of the ways interpretation of economic data depends on framing, comparison and context. Considers ways clarity and fairness in economic reporting are essential to public trust. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of corporate filings and financial disclosure; market trends, labor shifts and cost-of-living metrics; economic indicators such as inflation, housing or consumer confidence; industry case studies across sectors such as energy, technology, retail or health care; regulatory and policy developments; and narrative approaches to profiling companies, entrepreneurs or local businesses. Course material may involve coverage of contested issues such as corporate incentives, taxation policy, wage debates and/or market volatility. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Sports Entertainment Reporting
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines journalistic storytelling within the evolving sports entertainment landscape. Explores formats ranging from narrative features and long-form commentary to rapid-cycle blogging, podcasts and fan-centered analysis. Emphasizes audience engagement, platform-specific voice and the blending of reporting, opinion and personality in sports media. Simulates newsroom or creator environments through recurring publishing deadlines and performance-based feedback. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds marketable skills for careers in sports journalism, content creation, digital media, public relations or brand communications. Reinforces professional practices such as sourcing, accuracy, editorial decision-making, audience strategy and ethical judgment under time pressure. Supports civic and cultural awareness by examining how sports intersect with identity, economics, politics and public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports coverage functions not only as entertainment but also as storytelling that frames community, rivalry, aspiration and controversy. Reveals distinctions between reportage, commentary, satire and hype, clarifying how credibility and influence can be negotiated across formats. Informs reflection on how fandom, access and commercial pressures shape journalistic tone and judgment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and production of sports blogs, feature stories, commentary pieces, social media threads, podcasts and/or multimedia packages. Consideration of athlete branding and influencer culture; fan communities and online discourse; ethics in sports reporting; representation and identity in sports narratives; commercialization of collegiate and professional athletics. May reference real-world cases involving controversy, misconduct and/or public debate when relevant to understanding communication choices in sports media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Magazine Feature Writing
prereq_text: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced nonfiction storytelling skills through the study and production of magazine-length features, profiles, trend pieces, service journalism and/or first-person narratives. Emphasizes writing for publication across contemporary formats, including print, digital and/or multimedia environments. Involves pitching, researching, drafting and revising multiple feature-length articles under deadline, simulating professional editorial workflows. Includes analysis of publication style, voice and audience expectations across diverse magazine platforms. May involve coverage of current events or human-interest topics, approached through journalistic standards. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies used by staff and independent writers within journalism, content strategy and media production, including interviewing, audience analysis, query development, revision and editorial collaboration. Supports preparation for publication-based careers as well as academic and civic contexts requiring long-form narrative communication, evidence-based reporting and/or clear voice. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how narrative journalism blends factual reporting with structure, scene-setting, characterization and perspective to build engagement while maintaining accuracy and accountability. Illuminates how credibility is earned through transparency, sourcing and stylistic discipline rather than formulaic structure. Encourages reflection on the responsibilities of representing real people and events in written form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of profile writing, trend stories, service journalism, memoir and first-person features, pitch and query formats, magazine house style and voice, interviewing strategies, source documentation, revision techniques and editorial feedback processes. May involve field reporting, live story pitching and analysis of magazine departments or adopted publications. May draw on real-world reporting scenarios, ranging from lifestyle to public affairs, addressed with attention to fairness, accuracy and professional responsibility. Prerequisites: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Journalism as a Profession
prereq_text: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification; enrollment in JOUR major or JOUR minor; and approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Serves as an exit-level seminar for students completing advanced coursework in journalism. Synthesizes prior training in reporting, writing, editing, media law and ethics by requiring production of publication-quality work alongside critical reflection on journalism as a profession. Combines workshop-based writing development with discussion of contemporary issues facing news media, including questions of credibility, labor, technology and/or public trust. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens readiness for careers in journalism, media production, strategic communication and public information by refining writing portfolios, pitching skills, professional presentation and editorial collaboration. Provides preparation for workplaces that value initiative, ethical decision-making and long-form project management. Supports civic literacy by deepening understanding of journalism’s role in public accountability, information access and democratic culture. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights journalism not only as a set of skills but as an evolving institution shaped by economic pressures, technological change, audience behavior and ethical norms. Encourages recognition of the practical and moral challenges journalists face when balancing accuracy with speed, objectivity with transparency and access with independence. Reinforces that credibility emerges through verification, sourcing, clarity and sustained commitment to public responsibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include discussions of media credibility, fact-checking in high-risk environments, newsroom labor and diversity, long-form storytelling, press freedom, branding and career sustainability and journalistic responses to misinformation. May contain real-world reporting cases involving political conflict, legal disputes or sensitive human experiences, examined for purposes of professional analysis. Prerequisites: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification; enrollment in JOUR major or JOUR minor; and approval of instructor.

subject: KINE
title: The Art of Movement
description: Examine and appreciate movement as expressed by every culture, recognizing that movement is shaped by practical and artistic contexts. Through application, examine how dance is used to advance personal and social expression through design, patterning, connoted meaning and interconnected form. Dance is analyzed through multiple activities, including attending and critiquing a live dance performance, to enhance perspective, experience and appreciation of dance movement.

subject: KINE
title: Introduction to the Science of Health and Fitness
description: Overview of the human body systems. Interdisciplinary focus on wellness, exercise, nutrition, disease and drug use. Integrated kinesthetic lessons with physical activity and lab experiences that center on the scientific principles and application of conditioning. Through a variety of topics that relate to health, wellness and exercise, students will collect data, evaluate the information and formulate plans based on the findings. Application based experiences will be completed using a blend of equipment, software and technology to collect and evaluate data; also taught at Galveston campus.

Prerequisite: Approval of Instructor.

title: Digital Fundamentals for Marine Engineers
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 , ECEN 215 , or ESET 210 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Marine digital systems and applications including logic and devices that enable these applications throughout many industries; fundamentals and basic concepts of number systems, Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinatorial and sequential logic design, and digital electronics; examination of modern digital devices used for computing, automation, system monitoring, and control. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 , ECEN 215 , or ESET 210 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARE
title: Fluid Mechanics Theory
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Theory of incompressible and compressible fluid flow, introduction to fluid power systems and controls, and dynamics of turbomachinery. Mathematical analysis of piping systems to determine pump head, system resistance, and pipe sizing optimization. Topics include physical properties of fluids, continuity equation, Bernoulli's Equation, Darcy's Equation, series and parallel flow, relative roughness, friction factors, dimensional analysis, and laws of similitude. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARE
title: Electrical Power II
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 .
description: Electrical power generation and distribution; AC and DC rotating machinery; transformers; controllers and safety devices; operation, maintenance and repair procedures and practices; static converters AC/DC and DC/AC that are used in modern electric propulsion systems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 .

subject: MARE
title: Marine Electronics
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 .
description: Introduction to the theory of electronic circuits. Fundamentals and basic concepts of semiconductors; solid-state components; power supplies; amplifiers; inverters; rectifiers; oscillators; digital and analog integrated circuits. Application in automation, motor controllers, battery-charging systems, communications; and propulsion plant monitoring systems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MARE 207 .

subject: MARE
title: Marine Construction Materials
prereq_text: CHEM 107 and CHEM 117 .
description: Introduction to materials science and engineering, structural, property relationships; advanced manufacturing techniques from the point of view of marine applications such as subsea pipelines, ship hulls, etc.; corrosion and biofouling. Laboratory includes experimental testing of materials properties, materials syntheses and heat treatment techniques. Prerequisite: CHEM 107 and CHEM 117 .

subject: MARE
title: Diesel Propulsion Plants
prereq_text: CHEM 107 ; grade of C or better in MARE 202 .
description: Comprehensive study of diesel engines, thermodynamics of air standard cycles, actual compression ignition engine cycles, emissions and emission controls, fuel injection systems and turbo charging systems, engine material properties, operational parameters including forces and temperatures resulting from combustion and inertial dynamics. Laboratory includes computer-aided parametric analysis of engine performance and use of low-speed diesel propulsion plant simulator. Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Prerequisites: CHEM 107 ; grade of C or better in MARE 202 .

subject: MAST
title: Introduction to Museums and Conservation
description: Introduction to museums, cultural heritage and collections care; best practice for non-profit institutions, public engagement, and the collection, preservation and exhibition of material culture; emphasis on archaeological, ethnographic and historical collections, or other collections of cultural significance.

subject: MAST
title: Museums, Law and Ethics
description: Exploration of museum law and ethics; interdisciplinary topics.

subject: MAST
title: Maritime Folklore
description: Maritime folklore tales and myths; monsters and mysteries of the sea.

subject: MAST
title: Introduction to Maritime Studies
description: First year experience; exploration of Maritime Studies; interdisciplinary topics.

subject: MAST
title: Historic Seafaring and Maritime Heritage
description: Fundamentals of traditional seamanship and an exploration of the cultures and technologies of seafaring people throughout history and in various geographical locations.

subject: MAST
title: Historic Seafaring and Maritime Heritage

subject: MAST
title: Viking Archaeology and Norse Mythology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classificaiton or approval of instructor.
description: Overview of Viking Age (ca. 800 to 1100 C.E.) in Northern Europe; topics include Norse seafaring, world-view, society, archaeology, religion and cosmology as know from the archaeological and literary record. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classificaiton or approval of instructor.

subject: MAST
title: Maritime Foreign Policy
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Strategies used by governments to guide international actions; objectives of state leaders in decision making; sources, processes, objectives and outcomes of maritime policy choices. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MAST
title: Texas Maritime Culture and History
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: The coastal peoples, maritime history and culture of the Texas Gulf Coast ranging from pre-historic times to the present day; geography's influence on exploration, resources utilization, development and inland access; Texas ports historic and modern; shipwreck sites and historical texts; La Salle's La Belle, Texas Navy, Mexican War logistics; Civil War Naval actions, Texas Fisheries, tourism and recreation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: MAST
title: Ancient Egyptian Seafaring
prereq_text: ANTH 316 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Archaeology, iconography and written records of ancient Egypt as they relate to local and international trade by land, river and sea, beginning in Neolithic times (c. 5000 B.C.) to the end of the New Kingdom (c. 1069 B.C.). Prerequisites: ANTH 316 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MAST
title: Material Culture
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Examination of material evidence of human life, from cradles to graves, churches to forts, teapots to landscapes; material culture artifacts, the processes and technologies used to create them and their use in every day life; application to archaeology, museum studies and basic engineering. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MAST

subject: MAST
title: Collections Care and Management
prereq_text: MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Managing collections in libraries, archives and museums; media and collections storage; digitization and metadata processes; use of writing styles and citations. Prerequisites: MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MAST
title: International Maritime Culture
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Explores diverse maritime cultures across varied geographic regions along with their social practices, economic activities and cultural beliefs as well as the contemporary challenges that confront these communities. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: MAST
title: Thesis and Technical Writing
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; ENGL 104 and ENGL 203 or ENGL 210 .
description: Rhetorical techniques for professional expository prose; intertextual argumentation and analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; ENGL 104 and ENGL 203 or ENGL 210 .

subject: MAST
title: Maritime Piracy
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
description: Research of social, economic, political and cultural aspects of piracy from ancient to modern times; presentation of findings; understanding modern perception of pirates through modern art, literature and movies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: MAST
title: Advanced Museum Studies
prereq_text: MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification.
description: Exploration of advanced topics in museum programs; preservation, research, education, outreach; development and implementation; emphasis on historical contexts, disciplinary intersections, ethical obligations and professional responsibilities; service to community, state and national interest and advancement of sciences. Prerequisite: MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: MAST
title: Internship

description: Supervised study in a research or teaching laboratory remote from Texas A&M University at Galveston. Student involvement is to consist of real-life learning or research, teaching, management or a combination of these. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

prereq_text: High school algebra I and II and geometry; not open to senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: (MATH 1324) Mathematics for Business and Social Sciences. Application of common algebraic functions, including polynomial, exponential, logarithmic and rational, to problems in business, economics and the social sciences; includes mathematics of finance, including simple and compound interest and annuities; systems of linear equations; matrices; linear programming; and probability, including expected value. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: MATH 140 or MATH 168 . Prerequisites: High school algebra I and II and geometry; not open to senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

title: Business Calculus

description: (MATH 1325) Business Calculus. Limits and continuity; techniques and applications of derivatives including curve sketching and optimization; techniques and applications of integrals; emphasis on applications in business, economics, and social sciences. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 140 or MATH 150 , or equivalent or acceptable score on Texas A&M University math placement exam; not open to senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

prereq_text: Mechanical engineering major; grade of C or better in ENGR 102 .
description: Foundations of geometric modeling as applied to mechanical design through use of modern computer-aided design (CAD) and physical prototyping tools; basics of systematic design methodology; geometric visualization concepts: multiview orthographic, isometric, oblique, perspective; three-dimensional representations, surface and solid modeling; dimensioning and tolerancing; rapid prototyping using 3D printing. title: Alternative Energy Conversion
prereq_text: MEEN 315 .

title: Principles of Business Regulations and Law

description: Broad survey of international business issues; analyzes the environment in which international businesses operate; examines international economic issues including trade theory, investment theory, foreign exchange and capital markets, and balance of payments; introduces multinational enterprises, global competition, international organizations, treaties and international law, national trade policies and the determinants of competitiveness of firms in international markets. subject: MGMT
title: /IBUS 457 Global Entrepreneurship

Prerequisite: Admission to upper division in Mays Business School. Cross Listing: IBUS 457/MGMT 457 .

title: /SOCI 432 Technology Commercialization

description: Examination of the process of introducing to the marketplace new products or services based upon scientific and technological innovations; practical skills for assessing the technology, identifying potential products and services, and quantifying market demand; focuses on value creation, financing, intellectual property law, regulatory, and socio-economic drivers. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or admission to upper division in Mays Business School; SOCI 376/MGMT 376 or MGMT 376/SOCI 376 and SOCI 476/MGMT 476 or MGMT 476/SOCI 476 recommended. subject: MUST
title: Foundations of Museum Studies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums. Cross Listing: ANTH 221 and ARCH 221 .

subject: NURS
title: Transition to Professional Nursing Practice
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in NURS 305 , NURS 306 or NURS 313, NURS 307 or NURS 314, NURS 315 , NURS 320 , NURS 411 , NURS 412 , and NURS 420 .
description: Course reflects content that will prepare senior students for transition of entry into practice. Theories and principles concerning human behavior in organizations, with emphasis on leadership roles encountered in professional nursing practice. Senior nursing students in collaboration with nursing faculty refine coordination of care for a diverse population of clients. A clinical practicum will focus on synthesizing and refining skills in the delivery and management of nursing care to various groups of clients. Concepts of clinical decision-making, and inter-professional dynamics are incorporated in the context of legal, ethical, and evidence-based practice. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in NURS 305 , NURS 306 or NURS 313, NURS 307 or NURS 314, NURS 315 , NURS 320 , NURS 411 , NURS 412 , and NURS 420 .

subject: NURS
title: Nursing Dimensions and Informatics for the RN
description: This course is designed to build on the informatics knowledge and skills of the practicing nurse. Emphasis is placed on the application of the ANA Standards for Nursing Informatics and Professional Practice and incorporation of information technology to support patient care and clinical decision-making. The course will assist the students to develop the professional role by incorporation of the philosophy of nursing, nursing theory, and clinical reasoning. The nurse’s role in interprofessional practice will be explored. The influence of ethics and cultural/society issues on the nursing profession are explored as well as opportunities for personal and professional development.

description: Students will demonstrate the ability to incorporate the principles of pathophysiology and pharmacology in planning healthcare for individuals across the lifespan.

subject: NURS
title: Health Assessment for the RN
description: In this course, the concepts and principles underlying assessment of the health status of culturally diverse individuals are presented. An emphasis is placed on reviewing and renewing cognitive, affective, and psychomotor skills to obtain health histories and discover physical and psychosocial findings in the well person. The role of genetics in family histories is examined. Successful completion of the course requires students to successfully complete a head-to-toe health assessment examination with accurate documentation of the findings.

title: Health Promotion Across the Lifespan for the RN

subject: NURS
title: Community Health for the RN
description: In this course, students are introduced to community-based health care of culturally diverse populations. The role of the professional nurse as part of an interprofessional team in health promotion, disease prevention, and management of chronic health problems in community settings is explored. Students apply critical reasoning and information technology skills to develop and implement evidence-based projects that positively impact the quality of life of populations. Practicum experiences are individualized.

subject: NURS
title: Leadership and Management for the RN
description: In this course, theories and principles of human behavior in organizations are examined, including an exploration of leadership roles in professional nursing practice. The role of regulatory agencies in the provision of quality health care is explored. Students will participate in the evaluation and planning for quality improvement using nurse sensitive indicators. The students will discern the nurse’s role in reducing the financial cost of health care. Practicum experiences are individualized.

subject: OCNG
title: The Blue Planet - Our Oceans
description: (GEOL 1345, GEOL 1445*) The Blue Planet - Our Oceans. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces the ocean as a dynamic system that shapes our planet and our lives. You will explore how Earth processes like plate tectonics, oceanic and atmospheric circulation, climate and ecosystems are tied together by the ocean. description: (GEOL 1345, GEOL 1445*) The Blue Planet - Our Oceans. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces the ocean as a dynamic system that shapes our planet and our lives. You will explore how Earth processes like plate tectonics, oceanic and atmospheric circulation, climate and ecosystems are tied together by the ocean. Along the way, we will ask big questions about the role of the ocean in sustaining life, how humans affect the marine environment and how science can inform solutions to global challenges. Expect to engage with complex issues such as sustainability, climate change and human impacts, while also gaining a strong foundation in ocean science concepts that will help you navigate both the classroom and the world around you. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Understanding the ocean is not only exciting — it is essential. The ocean drives weather, climate and ecosystems that directly influence human life and the global economy. In this course, you will practice skills that matter well beyond the classroom: analyzing scientific data, working in teams, communicating scientific ideas and thinking critically about real-world problems. These tools will support your academic growth, prepare you for professional pathways and help you make informed decisions as a citizen in a world where the health of the ocean and society are deeply connected. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include plate tectonics and the seafloor, seawater properties, waves, tides, circulation and climate connections. You will study marine ecosystems and the relationships between ocean organisms and the adaptations needed to live in different oceanic regions, as well as the impact of humans on coasts and the open ocean. The course also highlights sustainability, sea level rise and ocean policy as they connect to global challenges. Class discussions and current events will add new perspectives, keeping the course timely and relevant; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: OCNG
title: The Blue Planet - Our Oceans Laboratory
description: Credit 1. 2 Lab Hours. (GEOL 1145, GEOL 1445*) The Blue Planet - Our Oceans Laboratory. COURSE OVERVIEW. This laboratory course introduces students to the study of the ocean through hands-on experiments, data collection and collaborative exploration. Students investigate key oceanographic processes such as seafloor mapping, salinity, density, ocean circulation and the biological and chemical dynamics of marine systems. Each lab encourages curiosity about how the ocean works and builds foundational scientific skills through direct observation, measurement and analysis. The course helps students connect ocean science concepts to the broader Earth system. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. This course gives students a practical understanding of ocean processes that influence weather, climate and life on Earth. The skills learned are essential in both scientific and everyday contexts. By engaging in experiments that mirror real-world oceanographic research, students learn how scientific knowledge is generated and applied to address issues such as sea level rise, ocean acidification and pollution. The experience strengthens scientific literacy and prepares students to make informed decisions as students, citizens and future professionals. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include bathymetry and seafloor structure, salinity and density, ocean circulation, sedimentation, plankton ecology, ocean acidification and human impacts on marine environments. Students develop a deeper appreciation for the interconnected nature of the ocean system and the role of human activity in shaping its future.

subject: OCNG
title: Professional Communication in Oceanography
prereq_text: OCNG 251 ; COMM 203 or COMM 205 ; OCNG or OCNS majors; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces students to critical skills in communicating marine science effectively through written and oral formats. Students will explore how scientific findings and knowledge are translated into relevant, impactful works when they are clearly conveyed to peers, policy makers and the public. Course activities and assignments include practicing the art of communicating scientific concepts to different audience types and building professional identities through career development. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Effective communication is a cornerstone of careers in marine science. Scientists must be able to translate complex ideas into accessible language whether they are conducting research, advocating for policy or educating the public. This course equips students with the skills necessary to write and speak with purpose and clarity, with the goal of elevating students’ academic achievements and preparing them to enter the workforce. Students will be exposed to various pathways in marine and aquatic sciences and gain insight into how communication skills will prepare them for future careers, studies and leadership positions. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Students will learn about scientific writing styles for different audiences, strategies for delivering oral presentations and techniques for telling engaging scientific narratives. Assignments and topics covered in class will include how to write compelling abstracts, reports to inform policymakers, and develop outreach materials. In-class discussions will incorporate emerging issues in ocean science and methods for effective peer review. The course includes professional development, where students will build their resumes, practice writing cover letters and participate in mock interviews. Prerequisites: OCNG 251 ; COMM 203 or COMM 205 ; OCNG or OCNS majors; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Physical Oceanography
prereq_text: MATH 152 ; PHYS 206 ; PHYS 226 , PHYS 216/ENGR 216 , or ENGR 216/PHYS 216 ; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces the fundamental physical processes that govern the ocean and its interactions with the atmosphere. Students will explore the physical properties of seawater, the forces that drive ocean circulation and the mechanisms that shape ocean dynamics across scales — from small-scale turbulence to basin-wide currents. Through lectures, problem-solving and case studies, the course builds a foundation in the principles of physical oceanography, including kinematics, hydrostatics, stability, Coriolis effects, geostrophy, wave motions and tides. By the end of the semester, students will be equipped with conceptual and analytical tools to interpret ocean phenomena and evaluate their role in the Earth system. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Understanding the physics of the ocean is essential for addressing some of the most pressing scientific and societal challenges of our time. Ocean circulation regulates climate, drives weather patterns and influences ecosystems and fisheries. Processes such as upwelling, mixing and thermohaline circulation play critical roles in distributing heat, carbon and nutrients across the globe. Students will also gain skills in interpreting observational data, applying mathematical models and placing local oceanographic events in a global context — skills that are increasingly valuable in research, industry, policy and environmental decision-making. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Ocean-atmosphere interactions — heat, momentum and freshwater fluxes; tropical storms; ENSO and other oscillations; physical properties of seawater — temperature, salinity, density, stratification and water masses; forces and dynamics — gravity, pressure, Coriolis force, geostrophy, wind-driven circulation and thermohaline processes; ocean circulation and transport — currents, upwelling, downwelling, mixing, diffusion and subduction; waves and tides — surface waves, internal waves, Langmuir circulation, rogue waves, tsunamis and tidal dynamics; climate and change — sea-level rise, carbon and heat uptake and the role of the ocean in long-term climate variability; regional and applied oceanography — coastal processes, Gulf of Mexico dynamics and contemporary case studies from oceanography in the news. Prerequisites: MATH 152 ; PHYS 206 ; PHYS 226 , PHYS 216/ENGR 216 , or ENGR 216/PHYS 216 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: OCNG
title: Geological Oceanography
prereq_text: OCNG 251 , GEOL 101 or GEOG 203 , or approval of instructor.
description: This course introduces the geological processes that shape our ocean basins and influence the marine environment. You will explore how plate tectonics, mid-ocean ridges and geological processes at ocean margins create key features of the world’s surface and exert great influence on ocean circulation, the distributions of life in the oceans, chemical cycling at the earth surface and global climate. You will discover how we use geophysical techniques to image the oceans and geological sampling methods to discover the information about the marine environment. You will explore the histories of marine life and Earth’s environment recorded by marine sediments and other geological features. You will develop an appreciation of the practical consequences that marine geological processes have for human society in the coastal zone, as well as the invaluable information about past climate, sea level fluctuations and natural hazards such as earthquakes that offer of society an essential perspective for anticipating and making informed decisions as we develop plans for our future. Prerequisites: OCNG 251 , GEOL 101 or GEOG 203 , or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Chemical Oceanography
prereq_text: CHEM 120 and OCNG 251 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces the chemical structure and functioning of the ocean as a critical component of the Earth system. You will explore the major and trace chemical constituents of seawater, their sources and sinks and the processes that control their distribution and reactivity. The course emphasizes the interactions between chemistry, biology, physics and geology that determine the composition and behavior of seawater. Key questions include: How do physical properties and ocean circulation influence chemical distributions? What governs the cycling of nutrients and gases? How do redox reactions and microbial metabolisms shape marine environments? You will engage in problem-solving, quantitative analysis and data interpretation through lectures, discussions and lab-based exercises. The course challenges students to connect molecular-scale reactions to global patterns and to consider how ocean chemistry both influences and responds to human-driven environmental change. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. The chemistry of the ocean plays a central role in regulating Earth’s climate, sustaining life and buffering human impacts. Understanding these processes is essential for interpreting climate change, predicting ocean acidification, managing marine resources and maintaining ecosystem health. This course provides a foundation for advanced study in oceanography, marine biology, environmental science and geochemistry. Students develop quantitative skills relevant to laboratory and field research, environmental monitoring and data-driven decision-making. Beyond professional preparation, the course fosters scientific literacy and critical thinking about the chemical links between the ocean, atmosphere and human activity. By connecting ocean chemistry to global challenges, students gain tools to engage in evidence-based reasoning and contribute to sustainable solutions in their communities and careers. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include the composition and properties of seawater, salinity, residence time and conservative vs. non-conservative elements, gas exchange and the role of the ocean in atmospheric regulation, organic matter production, remineralization and nutrient cycling, redox reactions and biogeochemical pathways, carbonate chemistry and the ocean carbon system, nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and their role in biological productivity, anthropogenic carbon emissions and ocean acidification, quantitative techniques in marine chemistry and the integration of physical, chemical, geological and biological processes in the ocean. Prerequisites: CHEM 120 and OCNG 251 .

subject: OCNG
title: Marine Pollution
prereq_text: OCNG 251 , ENSS 105 , ATMO 201 , GEOL 101 or GEOG 203 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course provides a foundational understanding of the sources, fates and societal impacts of marine pollutants. Students will explore what constitutes pollution in the marine environment and examine the effects on humans and wildlife. Key concepts include bioaccumulation, biomagnification and the risks of emerging contaminants. The course emphasizes the interdisciplinary nature of marine pollution, preparing students to engage with complex environmental topics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Understanding marine pollution is essential for informed environmental stewardship. This course connects scientific principles to real-world issues by examining the laws and policies related to various pollutants. The knowledge gained prepares students for future studies, careers and active participation in environmental sciences and policies. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Through this course, students will examine a broad spectrum of pollutants and environmental stressors. Major themes include the impacts of plastics, oil and excess nutrients in the marine environment. The course covers chemical contaminants like metals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, as well as physical pollutants such as sediment input, sound and light. Additional topics include wastewater, pathogens, radiation, ocean acidification and changes in temperature and salinity. Prerequisite: OCNG 251 , ENSS 105 , ATMO 201 , GEOL 101 or GEOG 203 .

subject: OCNG
title: Ocean Observing Systems
prereq_text: OCNG 251 or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course investigates the rationale behind ocean observing systems by familiarizing students with the relevant social, scientific design, technology and policy issues associated with observing system technologies. You will explore the technical capabilities and live data streams of the most common ocean observing platforms in service globally and in US waters. You will also consider the role of government agencies, private industry and academic institutions in sustaining and integrating useful ocean observing products and services into the everyday lives of the general public and decision makers. As an upper-level course, students will be given the opportunity to explore an aspect of ocean observing that pertains to their specific interests and goals by producing a term paper on a relevant topic of their choice. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Real-time information from the ocean helps to save lives, protects coastal communities and economies and sustains coastal ecosystems. Sustained ocean observing will require a technically trained and skilled ocean knowledgeable workforce from a wide variety of disciplines and interests ranging from stakeholder and engagement, data processing and data management, web services and products, predictive models and instrumentation operation. Many public and private sectors require timely and accurate ocean and environmental data, which makes this field a stable career pathway. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include the historical rationale and motivation for coastal and global ocean observing systems, sampling and instrumentation strategies and backbone system design, national and international government agencies with ocean observing investment, ocean technologies, examples, gliders, ARGO, HF radar, ocean observatories, satellites, numerical models, policy considerations and the political aspects of ocean observing. Class discussions and current events will add new perspectives, keeping the course timely and relevant. Prerequisite: OCNG 251 or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Microbial Oceanography
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; OCNG 251 or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces the diversity and complexity of marine microorganisms and their role in the ocean and wider Earth system. The goal of microbial oceanography is to understand how microorganisms affect the structure and function of marine ecosystems. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Marine microorganisms play an essential role in providing ecosystem services that modern human societies depend on, such as marine fisheries and the removal of pollutants. Marine microorganisms play a major role in global biogeochemical cycles of chemical elements essential to life on Earth. On geological time scales marine microorganisms have shaped global climate and the composition of the atmosphere. While studying microbial oceanography, you will develop transferable skills, including data analysis, critical thinking and scientific communication. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Diversity of microorganisms in the ocean, the metabolisms of marine microorganisms, the modern molecular methods used to study marine microorganisms, how marine microorganisms drive the marine carbon and nitrogen cycles, the response of marine microorganisms to change such as global heating and ocean acidification, the past contribution of marine microorganisms to the oxygenation of the atmosphere and the evolution of modern marine ecosystems, societal relevance and impact of marine microorganisms. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; OCNG 251 or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Oceanographic Field and Laboratory Methods
prereq_text: OCNG 251 and CHEM 120 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course immerses students in the practice of oceanographic fieldwork and laboratory analysis. Students learn how to collect, prepare and analyze samples while developing a scientific understanding of ocean processes. They gain experience working with real data from research cruises and laboratory experiments, practicing both individual and team-based approaches to problem solving. The course emphasizes accuracy, safety and professionalism in oceanographic research and challenges students to think critically as they interpret data and communicate their findings. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. This course bridges classroom learning and real-world oceanographic applications by building skills directly used in environmental research and applied studies. Students connect theoretical knowledge to real-world data collection used by oceanographers, environmental agencies and research institutions. The experience helps prepare students for graduate study, oceanographic careers or any profession requiring quantitative reasoning, teamwork and data-driven decision-making. Through field trips and laboratory work, students develop confidence in measuring and analyzing common ocean parameters to understand and address marine and environmental challenges that affect communities and ecosystems. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include field sampling and data collection, laboratory analysis of seawater, error analysis and data quality control, instrument calibration and post-cruise data organization. Students explore the relationship between field and laboratory observations, focusing on accuracy, precision and reliability of measurements. Themes of safety, teamwork, critical thinking and effective scientific communication are integrated throughout the semester. Prerequisites: OCNG 251 and CHEM 120 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Mathematical Modeling of Ocean Climate
prereq_text: MATH 308 .
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Problem-based course in theoretical and computer techniques applied to mathematical solutions of ocean climate, including ocean circulation, climate variability, El Niño. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Understanding the mathematical and computational foundations of modeling ocean climate processes is essential for addressing pressing global challenges such as climate change, sea level rise and extreme weather events, as well as improving seasonal climate predictions related to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This course equips students with practical skills in quantitative modeling, data analysis and scientific computing that are highly transferable to careers in climate science, oceanography, environmental consulting, data science and policy analysis. By linking theoretical concepts with real-world applications, students learn how ocean-atmosphere interactions influence global and regional climate and how modeling tools can be used to interpret observations and project future climate states. The course emphasizes critical thinking, problem-solving and data-driven reasoning — skills valuable not only for scientific research but also for informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Major topics include the distinction between weather and climate, the role of the ocean in regulating Earth’s climate and the physical basis for climate modeling. Students explore the hierarchy of climate models — from simple energy balance models to comprehensive Earth system models — and the mathematical and numerical techniques underlying their development. Additional themes include understanding the difference between natural climate variability, such as ENSO, and long-term climate change. Emphasis is placed on hands-on modeling exercises and data analyses. Prerequisite: MATH 308 .

subject: OCNG
title: Hydrothermal Vents and Mid-Ocean Ridges
prereq_text: OCNG 251 ; BIOL 112 ; CHEM 120 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course delves into the science of mid-ocean ridges and hydrothermal vent systems, focusing on the geological, chemical and biological processes that define these unique ecosystems. Students will explore how plate tectonics shape the formation of hydrothermal systems, the chemistry of vent fluids and how vent organisms interact with their environment. The course examines the latest research on vent microbiology, symbioses and biogeochemistry, offering an interdisciplinary approach to understanding deep-sea life. Students should expect to engage with complex scientific data, develop critical thinking skills and contribute to discussions on the implications of human activities such as deep-sea mining on these fragile ecosystems. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. The study of hydrothermal vents is crucial for understanding the Earth's geochemistry, deep-sea ecology and the potential for life beyond our planet. By the end of the course, students will have gained a deep understanding of the interconnectedness of biological, chemical and geological systems in extreme environments. This knowledge has broad applications, from advancing marine conservation efforts to informing sustainable mining practices. Additionally, the analytical skills developed in this course, such as interpreting complex data sets and conducting literature reviews, will be valuable in future academic research, environmental consulting and positions within scientific or governmental organizations. The course also fosters a deeper appreciation for how oceanography, biology and chemistry intersect in real-world contexts, preparing students to engage in discussions on environmental policy and science communication. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include the formation of hydrothermal vent systems at mid-ocean ridges, the chemical composition of vent fluids and their spatiotemporal variability, the ecology of vent organisms and the role of microbial symbioses in sustaining vent ecosystems. Students will also study the impact of hydrothermal plumes on ocean chemistry and marine life, the technologies used to study vent environments and the ecological implications of anthropogenic activities such as deep-sea mining. Themes of interdisciplinary integration, sustainability and the exploration of life in extreme environments will guide the course structure, with opportunities for students to explore the latest research and real-world applications. Prerequisite: OCNG 251 ; BIOL 112 ; CHEM 120 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: MATLAB Programming for Ocean Sciences
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of the instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces students to computational methods used in oceanographic data analysis through MATLAB programming. It combines lectures and hands-on labs to build practical skills in data handling, visualization and scientific computation. Students learn how to write scripts, work with real oceanographic datasets and create visual representations. The course encourages problem-solving, trouble-shooting and independent learning as students apply coding techniques to real-world ocean data. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. This course provides valuable technical skills that are widely used in academic research, government agencies and private industry. Students gain experience with MATLAB oceanographic toolboxes that support data analysis and research in oceanography, climate science and other data-driven fields. By the end of the semester, students are prepared to process and visualize large datasets, skills that are transferable to future coursework, research projects and professional roles that require computational thinking. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include MATLAB programming fundamentals, data input and manipulation, visualization techniques and analysis of oceanographic datasets. Students explore the use of oceanographic toolboxes, mapping and time series analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of the instructor.

subject: OCNG
title: Advanced Oceanographic Data Analysis and Communication
prereq_text: OCNG 403 ; STAT 211 or STAT 303 ; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This capstone course leads you through the complete lifecycle of an oceanographic data analysis project, from defining clear objectives and selecting a dataset to conducting rigorous analysis and communicating results in professional formats. You will plan and manage a multi-week workflow, write a proposal, perform exploratory data analysis, synthesize findings and iteratively draft a minimum 4,000-word technical report and a polished oral presentation. Expect focused attention to data quality and limitations, the logic of analytical choices and precise scientific writing for diverse audiences. The course provides a structured framework of milestones, in class demonstrations, targeted feedback and practice talks so you can navigate each stage with confidence. You will also engage with academic integrity expectations and explicit guidance on when generative AI and other tools are permitted, how they must be cited and what constitutes unacceptable assistance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Turning complex observations into clear, defensible conclusions is essential for graduate study, research labs, agencies and industry. By executing an end to end analysis on a real dataset, you will strengthen high value skills in project planning and time management, quantitative exploration and synthesis, analytical writing and concise oral communication. These abilities transfer directly to thesis work, interdisciplinary collaboration, environmental reporting and stakeholder engagement, where transparent methods and clear visuals are vital. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Core themes include technical writing for science, project scoping, literature review and dataset identification aligned with well defined objectives. You will conduct exploratory data analysis to evaluate data quality, characterize uncertainty and outline advanced methods suited to your questions. The writing sequence develops strong background, methods, results and discussion sections supported by effective figures and tables. You will refine synthesis and interpretation into coherent conclusions and translate your report into an engaging talk through practice presentations and a final oral presentation to a professional audience. Throughout, you will apply feedback from in class demonstrations and hone the organization, analysis and communication skills required to handle complex oceanographic information with clarity and rigor. Prerequisites: OCNG 403 ; STAT 211 or STAT 303 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: OCNG
title: Python for Geosciences
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course introduces core Python programming for scientific applications, emphasizing one- and two-dimensional geospatial analysis, plotting and working with large geophysical datasets. Students learn modern programming practices, including object-oriented design, while building notebooks and scripts that read and write data, detect and handle errors and perform complete end-to-end analyses. The learning journey moves from fundamentals (data structures, loops, functions) to scientific libraries (NumPy, matplotlib, pandas, Cartopy, xarray) and a final project where students analyze a dataset of their choice. This course is open to students with no prior programming experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Python is a cornerstone of contemporary geoscience, climate, environmental data and data science workflows. This course cultivates workforce-ready skills — data ingestion, cleaning, analysis, visualization, mapping and communication — that transfer directly to research labs, government agencies, non-profits and industry roles. The final project strengthens portfolio-quality evidence of applied proficiency and prepares students for advanced study and data-driven decision-making in their communities. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key themes include reading and writing standard data formats; core language fluency with variables, containers, loops and functions; object-oriented programming; numerical computing with NumPy; 1D and 2D plotting with matplotlib; time series analysis with pandas; geospatial mapping with Cartopy and shapefiles; and working with NetCDF via xarray for local and remote datasets, with consistent attention to error identification and best practices in visualization and reproducible workflows. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
