subject: OCNG
title: Data Analysis Methods in Geosciences
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; MATH 151 ; STAT 211 , STAT 301, STAT 302 or STAT 303 , or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course examines how geoscientists conceptualize research questions, collect and process observations and apply statistical and computational methods to data drawn from environmental, atmospheric and oceanographic contexts. Students explore core questions such as how to select appropriate analytical techniques for different data types, how to quantify error and uncertainty and how to formulate and test hypotheses using real-world datasets. The course emphasizes hands-on programming in Python, R or MATLAB to build medium-length scripts that analyze, visualize and interpret geosciences data while developing reproducible workflows. Students should expect challenging, authentic problem-solving with messy data, rigorous model diagnostics and engagement with complex issues like experimental design, variance partitioning and responsible data management. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. The skills developed in this course are foundational for research in the geosciences and directly transferable to professional roles in environmental consulting, resource management, climate services, marine operations and public sector decision-making. By learning statistical analysis, visualization and programming, students gain tools to interpret real-world signals in noisy data, communicate evidence clearly and make informed, data-driven decisions. The emphasis on hypothesis testing, regression modeling, ANOVA and principal component analysis prepares students to evaluate claims, design robust studies and translate complex analyses into practical insights for stakeholders and communities. KEY TOPICS AND THEMES. Key topics include probability, hypothesis development, field study design with attention to replication, independence, and randomization, correlation and data visualization; linear and multiple regression, ANOVA and hypothesis testing. Students develop computational proficiency in Python, R or MATLAB; practice variance partitioning across regression, ANOVA and PCA; and build fluency in interpreting graphical and tabular representations of geosciences data. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; MATH 151 ; STAT 211 , STAT 301, STAT 302 or STAT 303 , or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
title: Introduction to Psychology
description: (PSYC 2301) Introduction to Psychology. Explore the scientific study of human behavior and mental processes through a broad overview of psychology’s core areas. Investigate topics such as brain function, sensation and perception, learning, memory, cognition, emotion, personality, development, social interaction and mental health. Examine how cultural, social, individual and biological factors shape thoughts, feelings and actions. Apply psychological theories to real-world situations involving relationships, decision-making, mental health and well-being. Evaluate research methods and ethical principles that guide psychological research. Strengthen critical thinking and communication skills while interpreting evidence, analyzing behavior and reviewing psychological phenomena. Gain insight into personal experiences, social dynamics and global perspectives through the lens of psychological science. Build a foundation for further study and professional success across diverse fields. Also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

subject: PBSI
title: /AFST 206 Black Psychology
description: Explore psychological science through the lens of African-descended peoples across the African Diaspora. Examine core psychological concepts, theories and methods from perspectives rooted in the Black experience. Analyze cultural assumptions in mainstream psychology, compare Afrocentric and Eurocentric frameworks and engage with Black epistemologies. Strengthen critical thinking, deepen cultural awareness and expand understanding of diverse psychological worldviews. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. Cross Listing: AFST 206/PBSI 206 .

subject: PBSI
title: Stereotypes, Prejudice and Minority Experience
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Analyze stereotyping, prejudice, discrimination and racism through psychological, historical, sociological and cultural perspectives. Examine how beliefs, attitudes and behaviors toward social groups are formed and maintained. Explore the lived experiences of marginalized groups. Apply scientific frameworks to understand intergroup dynamics and critically evaluate current social issues through the lens of psychological science. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 .

subject: PBSI
title: /AFST 209 Psychology of Culture and Diversity
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Explore how culture shapes psychological processes and how psychology explains cultural variation. Analyze cultural influences on cognition, emotion, motivation, identity and mental health. Examine the development and scientific study of culture and discuss how cultural contact and acculturation affect adaptation and intergroup relations. Apply psychological frameworks to understand global diversity and the dynamic relationship between individuals and their cultural environments. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 . Cross Listing: AFST 209/PBSI 209 .

subject: PBSI
title: /WGST 210 Psychological Aspects of Human Sexuality
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Examine human sexuality through biological, psychological, social, relational and cultural lenses. Analyze reproductive anatomy, gender roles, sexual identity, sexual orientation and sexual behavior across the lifespan. Explore topics including love, attraction, sexual health, sexual victimization, diversity and sexuality as a commodity. Apply the bio-psycho-social-cultural model to understand how various factors shape sexual experiences and attitudes. Develop skills to assess sexual health, promote well-being and articulate what healthy sexuality means. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 . Cross Listing: WGST 210/PBSI 210 .

subject: PBSI
title: Lifespan Development
description: (PSYC 2314) Lifespan Development. Explore human psychological development from conception through late adulthood, focusing on how individuals grow, change and adapt across life stages. Examine major theoretical perspectives and empirical research on emotional, cognitive, personality and social development. Investigate biological influences, cultural factors and social relationships that shape behavior and identity over time. Analyze key transitions such as infancy, adolescence, emerging adulthood and aging through evidence-based inquiry. Strengthen critical thinking and problem-solving skills while interpreting developmental claims using scientific methods. Gain insight into the dynamic interplay of nature and nurture and apply psychological principles to personal, professional and societal contexts.

subject: PBSI
title: Introduction to Behavioral and Cognitive Neuroscience
prereq_text: PBSI 107 or BIOL 111 .
description: Investigate the biological foundations of human thought, emotion and behavior through an introduction to cellular, behavioral and cognitive neuroscience. Examine how psychological processes emerge from neural structures and functions, integrating insights from cellular mechanisms to complex cognitive phenomena. Topics include neural anatomy and physiology, sensory and motor systems, sleep and circadian rhythms, emotion and stress, learning and memory, attention, language and mental disorders. Analyze current research and foundational theories using evidence from both human neuroscience techniques and animal models. Build a strong conceptual framework for understanding how brain activity supports cognition and behavior, preparing for advanced study in neuroscience, psychology and related disciplines. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 or BIOL 111 .

subject: PBSI
title: Survey of Industrial/Organizational Psychology
description: Explore the science and practice of industrial-organizational psychology, focusing on how psychological theory and principles apply to workplace behavior. Learn about evidence-based approaches to personnel and human resource management, including job analysis, recruitment, selection, training and performance evaluation. Gain knowledge about organizational topics such as motivation, leadership, teamwork, job satisfaction, organizational climate and occupational health. Compare psychological theory and empirical research to understand and improve individual and organizational outcomes.

subject: PBSI
title: /WGST 300 Psychology of Women
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Examine the psychological experiences of women across the lifespan through feminist, developmental and intersectional frameworks. Analyze how social, cultural, biological and psychological factors shape women’s roles and identities in diverse contexts. Explore key topics including gender development, media representation, sexual and reproductive health, cognitive and emotional functioning, work-family dynamics and mental and physical health. Investigate how intersecting identities—such as race, class, and disability—impact access, opportunity and psychological well-being. Strengthen critical thinking and apply evidence-based insights to real-world issues affecting women. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 . Cross Listing: WGST 300/PBSI 300 .

subject: PBSI
title: Elementary Statistics for Psychology
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PBSI 107 and PBSI 245 ; major in psychology.
description: Build foundational skills in statistical reasoning through the lens of psychological research. Learn to organize, summarize and interpret data using descriptive and inferential statistics. Apply statistical tests — including t-tests, ANOVA, correlation and regression — to psychology-based datasets. Strengthen understanding of reliability, validity and hypothesis testing. Compute key statistics both by hand and using statistical software to deepen conceptual understanding. Practice scientific writing and APA-style reporting in lab sessions. Develop analytical skills essential for evaluating research and communicating findings in psychology. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PBSI 107 and PBSI 245 ; major in psychology.

subject: PBSI
title: Research Design and Methods in Psychological Science
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PBSI 107 and PBSI 301 ; major in psychology.
description: Explore how psychological research is designed, conducted and evaluated using scientific and ethical principles. Investigate experimental and nonexperimental designs, emphasizing measurement, control and research validity. Critically assess threats to research validity. Examine psychometric properties such as reliability and validity. Apply statistical reasoning, as appropriate, to evaluate findings and become a critical consumer of psychological research published in peer-reviewed literature and popular press outlets. Strengthen scientific writing and analytical skills through hands-on practice and evidence-based evaluation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PBSI 107 and PBSI 301 ; major in psychology.

subject: PBSI
title: Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Explore the applied field of sport, exercise and performance psychology, examining how psychological principles influence physical performance, well-being and group and intergroup dynamics. Analyze core topics such as motivation, stress, anxiety, personality, leadership, team cohesion and psychological skills training. Investigate how these concepts apply not only to sport and exercise but also to broader performance domains including medicine, the performing arts, military, law enforcement and the workplace. Understand emerging career paths and applications of psychological science across diverse settings. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PBSI
title: Psychology of Adjustment and Personal Growth
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Apply psychological principles to understand and improve adjustment across individual, family, school, work and community settings. Explore personal growth, coping strategies and wellness across the lifespan, with attention to cultural, relational, individual and social influences. Examine topics such as stress, mental health, relationships, identity, diversity and life transitions. Practice assessing challenges and promoting change through evidence-based strategies. Strengthen skills in psychological evaluation, intervention and scientific communication to support well-being in everyday life. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PBSI
title: Psychology of Mental Health
prereq_text: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 301 and PBSI 302 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: Explore the scientific study of psychological disorders across the lifespan, focusing on how they are defined, assessed and treated. Examine core concepts in psychopathology including diagnostic classification, clinical assessment and research methods. Analyze biological, psychological and social factors contributing to conditions such as anxiety, mood, psychotic, eating and substance use disorders. Evaluate theoretical models and empirical evidence to understand the development and maintenance of psychological disorders. Strengthen critical thinking and prepare for advanced study in clinical science, mental health and related fields. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 301 and PBSI 302 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PBSI
title: Child Development
prereq_text: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 245 , MATH 140 , MATH 168 , MATH 142 , MATH 147 , MATH 151 , MATH 171 , MATH 152 , MATH 148 , MATH 172 , MATH 150 , PHIL 240 or STAT 201 .
description: Engage with foundational theories and contemporary research in developmental science. Investigate human development from prenatal stages through childhood, emphasizing physical, cognitive and socioemotional growth. Analyze developmental change through the lenses of core psychological perspectives like biopsychology, learning, memory, personality, emotion and social psychology. subject: PBSI
title: Social Psychology
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Explore how thoughts, feelings and behaviors are shaped by the presence of others through the lens of social psychology. Investigate major theories and research on topics such as social perception, attitudes and persuasion, conformity, group dynamics, prejudice, cultural influences, self and identity, aggression, prosocial behavior and interpersonal relationships. Analyze the power of social situations and group processes in shaping individual behavior. Apply psychological frameworks to interpret personal experiences, social interactions and broader societal patterns. Evaluate empirical findings and consider diverse perspectives to gain insight into the complexity of human behavior in social contexts. Strengthen critical thinking while developing a deeper understanding of how individuals influence and are influenced by others. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 .

subject: PBSI

prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: Explore the psychological dimensions of aging, including changes in physiology, memory, personality, emotional health and social relationships. Analyze how aging influences and is influenced by cultural attitudes, social stigmas and public policy. Examine late-life transitions and their impact on mental health and well-being. Apply psychological principles to real-world contexts such as clinical settings, family dynamics and media portrayals of aging. Develop insight into personal and societal experiences of aging across the lifespan. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 .

subject: PBSI
title: Forensic Psychology
prereq_text: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 306 recommended.
description: Explore the intersection of psychology and the legal system, focusing on how psychological theories, research and mental health expertise inform legal decision-making. Analyze the role of psychology in criminal trials, civil disputes and forensic evaluations. Examine how legal processes influence psychological practice and how psychological evidence contributes to justice outcomes. Engage with topics such as competency, criminal responsibility, eyewitness testimony, jury decision-making and the psychological impact of legal proceedings. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 306 recommended.

prereq_text: PBSI 107 ; approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
title: Behavioral Disorders of Children
prereq_text: PBSI 306 ; PBSI 307 or equivalent.
description: Behavior problems related to childhood; psychological aspects of mental retardation, emotional disturbance, physical handicaps and other disorders; causative factors, preventative and therapeutic methods explored; where feasible, practical experience included as requirement. Prerequisites: PBSI 306 ; PBSI 307 or equivalent.

subject: PBSI
title: Pain Psychology
prereq_text: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 302 and PBSI 360 recommended; junior or senior classification.
description: Critical and transdisciplinary approach to the study of pain including an examination of personal and historical conceptions of pain, understanding of biopsychosocial mechanisms of pain, and consideration of sociodemographic and global pain disparities. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 ; PBSI 302 and PBSI 360 recommended; junior or senior classification.

subject: PBSI
title: Psychology of Self
prereq_text: PBSI 107 or approval of instructor.
description: Explore the psychological science of the self, examining how individuals come to understand who they are and how that sense of self influences thoughts, emotions and behavior. Investigate core topics including self-concept, self-esteem, self-regulation, goals and social identities such as political, racial, religious, sexual, gender and national. Analyze the role of culture, social context and existential concerns — such as mortality and uncertainty — in shaping the self. Engage with research from cognitive, social, developmental and clinical psychology to understand the self as both a scientific construct and a central aspect of human experience. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
title: Principles of Behavior Change
prereq_text: 9 hours of psychology; PBSI 107 ; junior or senior classification; PBSI 301 and PBSI 302 recommended.
description: Explore the principles of behavior through the lens of behavioral psychology, including behaviorism, applied behavior analysis and behavior modification. Analyze how organisms learn and how these learning principles apply to human experiences. Examine foundational concepts such as reinforcement, punishment and stimulus control and evaluate their use in behavior therapy and real-world behavior change. Develop insight into how scientific methods are used to understand and influence behavior. Prerequisites: 9 hours of psychology; PBSI 107 ; junior or senior classification; PBSI 301 and PBSI 302 recommended.

subject: PBSI
title: Existential Psychology
prereq_text: PBSI 107 .
description: . Study of major theoretical perspectives and contemporary research in existential psychology; focus on theory and research examining major topics in existential psychology including the causes and consequences of mortality awareness, self-knowledge, authenticity, belief in free-will and the experience of meaning in life. subject: PBSI
title: Hormones and Behavior
prereq_text: PBSI 235 , PBSI 340 , VIBS 277 , or NRSC 277, or approval of instructor.
description: Principles of hormones and the endocrine system; relationships among hormones, the nervous system and a variety of behaviors in vertebrates including humans. Prerequisites: PBSI 235 , PBSI 340 , VIBS 277 , or NRSC 277, or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
title: Psychological and Social Determinants of Health Disparities
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Examine psychological, social, cultural and societal contributors to health disparities in the United States. Analyze how macrosocial factors — such as socioeconomic status, discrimination, gender, religion and geography — affect physical and mental health through mechanisms like stress, healthcare access and cultural inputs. Explore historical and contemporary patterns of morbidity and mortality using interdisciplinary research from psychology, sociology, public health and behavioral science. Strengthen critical thinking and scientific writing while evaluating conceptual models and empirical evidence. Topics and focal groups will vary by instructor. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Critically analyze primary literature to uncover theoretical and empirical insights, identify gaps in current research and generate innovative questions. Learn to apply methods such as hierarchical regression and ANCOVA in applied settings. Explore methods such as exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling and logistic regression to uncover insights from workplace data. Discuss the design and implementation of organizational surveys, evaluating item quality and data integrity. Strengthen the ability to integrate conceptual knowledge with practical software tools to support evidence-based decision making in professional settings. Prerequisites: PBSI 652 ; graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Engage with psychometric principles such as reliability, validity, Item Response Theory and bias detection to ensure high-quality assessments. Apply advanced methods such as multi-group confirmatory factor analysis to evaluate and refine organizational assessments. Learn to conduct complex statistical analysis, learning not only the theoretical foundations but also how to conduct these analyses using statistical software. Integrate psychometric theory and analytical evidence to support evidence-based decisions across diverse organizational contexts. Prerequisites: PBSI 652 ; PBSI 653 ; graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Contemporary Moral Issues
description: (PHIL 2306) Contemporary Moral Issues. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students evaluate the claims, presuppositions and reasoning of various positions, including one’s own, on contemporary social problems and analyze those problems using ethical and social theories. Students examine how ideas, values and other aspects of culture (including power and authority) shape and are shaped by human experience and institutions. Students practice respectful and thoughtful engagement on contentious matters, such as abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, the relationship between ethics and religion, violence and war, animal ethics, sexual morality, gender issues, health care ethics, equality and discrimination, biotechnology and bioengineering, economic injustice, climate ethics and global hunger and poverty, among others; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: (PHIL 1301) Introduction to Philosophy. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students are introduced to perennial and central topics in philosophy such as the good life and happiness, the problem of death, the existence of God, the nature of reality, the relationship of mind and body, the scope and limits of knowledge, the foundations of ethical life and moral judgment, the individual and the community, and the place of the human being in the cosmos. Students critically consider how ideas, values and other aspects of culture shape human experience. Students develop a deeper understanding of their individual responsibilities and become more effective in engaging in a variety of cultural contexts. Instructors may organize the course either by central figures in the history of philosophy or by topic; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: (PHIL 1301) Introduction to Philosophy. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students are introduced to perennial and central topics in philosophy such as the good life and happiness, the problem of death, the existence of God, the nature of reality, the relationship of mind and body, the scope and limits of knowledge, the foundations of ethical life and moral judgment, the individual and the community, and the place of the human being in the cosmos. Students critically consider how ideas, values and other aspects of culture shape human experience. Students develop a deeper understanding of their individual responsibilities and become more effective in engaging in a variety of cultural contexts. Instructors may organize the course either by central figures in the history of philosophy or by topic; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Ethics in a Digital Age
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore the interplay between ethical and social theories, principles, and values, and the interconnected digital world, on concerns related to topics such as artificial intelligence, social media, intellectual property, privacy, surveillance, cybercrime and cyberwarfare, internet governance, computing professionalism and cyber policy and law. Students reflect on whether and how traditional moral conceptions (e.g., on the good life, personal and civic responsibility and virtues) have been transformed. Students examine how ideas, values and other aspects of culture (including power and authority) shape and are shaped by human experience and institutions. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware engagement to prepare them to navigate a variety of cultural environments; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Directed Studies
prereq_text: Approval of department head.
description: Directed studies in specific problem areas of philosophy. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Natural Science
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate scientific methods and achievements. Students examine the nature and types of explanation, discovery, confirmation, models and theories. Discussions may touch on questions such as: How sound are our reasons to think that accepted theories are better than rejected theories? What is required for something to be explained scientifically? How do we demarcate science from pseudoscience? For example, what is the status of Creation Science? Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Social Science
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate the nature and objectivity of the social sciences, their paradigms and patterns of explanation. Students explore questions such as: Are there explanatory laws in the social sciences? Should social explanations always include information about individuals or can social facts by themselves be explanatory? What does the reproducibility crisis in the social sciences tell us? Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Art
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students read texts that examine fundamental questions about the creation of art, the nature of beauty and aesthetic experience. Possible themes for exploration include the relationship of art to morality, the role of art in society and the impetus for artistic production. Classes may treat these themes through contemporary writings, through an historical approach that engages thinkers in the history of philosophy or by examining specific art forms. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Social and Political Philosophy
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Philosophy challenge students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate key questions, concepts and debates in social and political thought, including those that were particularly influential on the founding generation of the United States. Sources include canonical primary texts but may also encompass more contemporary or critical responses to the canon. Emphasis is on fundamental problems in political life and may include: the source of political authority, the just distribution of the burdens and benefits of social life, the limits of state authority, the essence of political community, citizenship or responsibilities of civic life. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students examine the concept of evil through the medium of film, exploring how cinema reflects, interprets and interrogates philosophical understandings of morality, suffering and human nature. subject: PHIL
title: Ethics and Engineering
prereq_text: Junior classification.
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore ethical and social theories, principles and engineering codes of ethics and their application to ethical challenges faced by engineers. Students engage with issues, such as satisfying responsibilities to an employer, client, fellow employees, one’s profession and the public; managing project pressures, risks, liability, regulations and environmental concerns. Students practice resolving challenges that arise from varying norms found in international and cross-cultural initiatives, especially on gifts, bribes and extortion. Students critically consider the ways engineers and engineering change the human experience, cultures and the environment. Students practice respectful and thoughtful dialogue on contemporary issues, become aware of their own perspectives and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they can competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Coursework focuses on independent ethical analysis of real and hypothetical cases and on the techniques that can be used to evaluate them. Prerequisite: Junior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification.
description: Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders. Overview of the underlying science of human health and disease, considering biological mechanisms in the individual and in populations; topics include a broad set of categories of adverse health events: infectious and chronic diseases, exposure to pathogens and toxins, nutritional deficiencies, child and maternal health, biological bases of mental and behavioral health and addiction; examination of the interactions between biologic and sociocultural factors and the biology of epidemics; foundational understanding of opportunities to promote and protect health across the life course; application of disease knowledge in community and allied health professions. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification.

subject: POLS
title: The Mass Media and Politics
prereq_text: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements. Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 302 and JOUR 302 .

title: Leadership in Public Service
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PSAA 210 ; PSAA major or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.
description: This course provides abstract theoretical and real-world practical approaches to leadership, the study of leadership and its application in the public service sector and/or other settings where leadership is required. This course studies leadership models, styles and practices highlighting the paradigm shift from the industrial age to the information age. This course focuses on the characteristics of leaders important to effective leadership outcomes, cross-cultural skills essential for effective leadership in international and culturally diverse settings, self-assessment and the development of a personal leadership vision, and the strategic skills necessary for providing vision and strategic direction of the organization. This course challenges students to reflect on personal experiences, seek out information on how to become more effective leaders and construct a leadership journey map for ongoing growth and development beyond the classroom. This course is broken into four blocks of instruction: leadership traits and principles, applied leadership, leadership ethics and leadership development. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PSAA 210 ; PSAA major or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.

subject: PSAA
title: Public and Nonprofit Budgeting
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PSAA 210 and PSAA 340/POLS 340 ; PSAA major or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.
description: This course provides an in-depth examination of the theories and practices of budgeting for public and nonprofit organizations, emphasizing the role of budget as a planning and management tool for the strategic allocation of scarce resources. In this course, students will have the opportunity to gain a comprehensive understanding of budget formats and budget processes, encompassing preparation, approval and execution, as well as revenue structures, capital budgeting, debt management across federal, state and local governments and the nonprofit sector. Through the analysis of real-world case studies and hands-on exercises utilizing Excel and practitioner-oriented workbooks, students will develop the technical skills necessary to manage organizational resources effectively. The course emphasizes technical proficiency in revenue forecasting, calculating budget variance and interpreting complex budgeting information to ensure the responsible stewardship of public resources. By the end of the semester, students will be equipped to navigate budgetary challenges, communicate findings through concise reporting and make informed decisions that advance organizational goals and public interests. subject: PSAA
title: Leading and Managing Public Service Organizations

description: The course provides an in-depth exploration of the core principles and the fundamentals of effectively leading people, teams and organizations by applying essential organizational behavior and leadership theories. The course provides a broad foundation in organizational analysis, including organizational culture, group behavior, communication and change management while specifically examining their practical applications in public and nonprofit organizations. In this course, students will explore different leadership styles and management approaches to decision-making processes that align with public service values, integrity and ethics. Skill development is a central focus, covering competencies such as motivation, coaching, teamwork, empowerment and conflict resolution. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, the course’s case studies and classroom discussions focus specifically on the public and nonprofit organizations, requiring students to propose administrative and policy solutions for complex management problems. subject: RELS
title: /COMM 257 Communication, Religion and the Arts
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross Listing: COMM 257/RELS 257 .

prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: ANTH 317/RELS 317 .

title: /ANTH 403 Anthropology of Religion
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: ANTH 403/RELS 403 .

subject: RELS
title: /COMM 480 Religious Communication
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 480/RELS 480 .

subject: SCSC
title: Crop Biology and Physiology
prereq_text: SCSC 205 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
description: Emphasis on seed biology, germination, development of cells and tissues, anatomy, and growth and development of crop plants; plant hormones and tropisms, membranes and membrane transport, water absorption and transport through plants, photosynthesis, respiration and carbohydrate metabolism, and flowering; environmental effects on crop adaptation, growth, development, and productivity. Prerequisites: SCSC 205 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: SCSC
title: Water in Soils and Plants
prereq_text: SCSC 301 ; junior or senior classification; knowledge of college-level algebra; or approval of instructor.
description: Introduction to the physics of the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum; focus on soil, its physical properties and their interactions with water and weather in terrestrial ecosystems; examination of processes including precipitation, rainfall interception, raindrop impact, infiltration, runoff, drainage, soil water storage, evaporation, transpiration, solar radiation partitioning, soil temperature and heat transfer near the land surface; interactions of these processes with plant growth, solute transport, water quality and greenhouse gas emissions are considered; quantitative analysis is emphasized with applications in soil and environmental science, agronomy, ecology, hydrology and climatology. Prerequisites: SCSC 301 ; junior or senior classification; knowledge of college-level algebra; or approval of instructor.

subject: SCSC
title: Soil Morphology and Interpretations
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Field study of morphological features of soil profiles and the morphological characterization of soils concerning interpretation for soil use and management. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: SCSC
title: Principles of Crop Production
prereq_text: SCSC 105 or SCSC 205 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
description: Origin and development of major U.S. agronomic crops; crop and species adaptation; crop management factors such as cultivar selection, planting, pest control, plant nutrition, irrigation, harvesting; organic farming; conservation agriculture; bioenergy crops; influence of markets, government policies, and global economy on cropping strategies; provide an understanding of the major row and drill (agronomic) crops grown in the United States including barley, corn, cotton, grain sorghum, peanuts, rice, soybean and wheat. Prerequisites: SCSC 105 or SCSC 205 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: SCSC
title: Professional Development in Turfgrass
prereq_text: SCSC 302 or registration therein.
description: Credit 1. 2 Lab Hours. Includes but not limited to fertilizer, pesticide, irrigation calculations; turfgrass, insect and weed identification and management, soils and rootzone construction; irrigation system operation and auditing; sprayer and spreader operation and calibration; builds upon and allows application of information obtained in SCSC 302 ; designed to better prepare those intending to compete in the GCSAA and STMA Collegiate Turf Bowl competitions. Prerequisite: SCSC 302 or registration therein.

Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: SCSC
title: Soil and Water Microbiology Laboratory
prereq_text: SCSC 405 or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: Credit 1. 2 Lab Hours. Hands-on experience with current techniques for examining the types, numbers, activity and roles of soil and water microorganisms with specific application to the carbon, nitrogen and sulfur cycle; plant-microbial interactions; soil and water quality. subject: SEFB
title: Clinical Teaching I - Collaborative Practices in Education to Support Students with Disabilities
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in INST 210 ; admission to professional phase of program; or approval of instructor.
description: Field-based study of collaborative partnerships used in education to support students with disabilities; topics include best-practices in collaboration and effective co-teaching strategies; collaboration between professionals such as special educators, general educators, paraprofessionals, related service professionals, community agencies, and with families. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in INST 210 ; admission to professional phase of program; or approval of instructor.

subject: SEFB
title: Clinical Teaching II - Academic Data-Based Interventions
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in SEFB 315 ; SPED 325 or concurrent enrollment; admission to the professional phase of program.
description: Field-based study of evidence-based academic interventions for students who are at-risk or who have disabilities; includes response to intervention (RTI)/multi-tier systems of supports (MTSS) strategies, data driven decision-making with assessments, data collection, selection of interventions, applying interventions, and progress monitoring used in school-based settings. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in SEFB 315 ; SPED 325 or concurrent enrollment; admission to the professional phase of program.

subject: SEFB
title: Clinical Teaching III - Specialized Instruction in High Support Needs
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in SEFB 325 and SPED 325 ; SPED 410 or concurrent enrollment; admission to professional phase of program.
description: Overview of learning and behavioral characteristics of individuals with low-incidence disabilities such as intellectual disability, autism, physical disabilities, traumatic brain injury, sensory impairments, and multiple disabilities; research-based practices in assessment, instructional strategies, collaboration, and designing educational environments that facilitate active participation, self-advocacy, and independence. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in SEFB 325 and SPED 325 ; SPED 410 or concurrent enrollment; admission to professional phase of program.

subject: SOCI
title: Introduction to Sociology
description: (SOCI 1301) Introduction to Sociology. Overview of sociology; provides theoretical knowledge and interpersonal and analytical skills used in careers like business, education, healthcare, law and law enforcement, nonprofits, social services and public policy; uses critical thinking and analysis skills as well as teamwork and ethical and civic awareness to study everyday interactions and foster a deeper understanding of human society in order to navigate the interconnected world using an evidence-based understanding. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise; also taught at Galveston campus.

Overview of sociology; provides theoretical knowledge and interpersonal and analytical skills used in careers like business, education, healthcare, law and law enforcement, nonprofits, social services and public policy; uses critical thinking and analysis skills as well as teamwork and ethical and civic awareness to study everyday interactions and foster a deeper understanding of human society in order to navigate the interconnected world using an evidence-based understanding. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: SOCI
title: /WGST 205 Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Studies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. The course focuses on current scholarship addressing the social construction of sex, sexuality and gender; institutional ways in which homophobia, biphobia and transphobia are systematically deployed; histories and examples of LGBTQ+ activism; evolution of desire and subjectivity; and the contributions of queer scholarship in understanding society. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings that address queer approaches to institutions; intersections of sexual and gender identity with race, class, ability/disability and/or nationality; digital activism; gender violence; controversies related to LGBTQ+ issues and politics, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Cross Listing: WGST 205/SOCI 215 .

prereq_text: SOCI 230 .
description: Basic ideas of contemporary sociological theory: structuralism, functionalism, conflict, symbolic interaction, exchange and their application to current research. Prerequisite: SOCI 230 .

subject: SOCI
title: /MGMT 479 Technology Commercialization
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or admission to upper division in Mays Business School; SOCI 376/MGMT 376 or MGMT 376/SOCI 376 and SOCI 476/MGMT 476 or MGMT 476/SOCI 476 recommended.
description: Examination of the process of introducing to the marketplace new products or services based upon scientific and technological innovations; practical skills for assessing the technology, identifying potential products and services, and quantifying market demand; focuses on value creation, financing, intellectual property law, regulatory, and socio-economic drivers. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or admission to upper division in Mays Business School; SOCI 376/MGMT 376 or MGMT 376/SOCI 376 and SOCI 476/MGMT 476 or MGMT 476/SOCI 476 recommended. Cross Listing: MGMT 479/SOCI 432 .

subject: SOCI
title: Sociology of Law
description: Introduction to the sociology of law; the relation of law to general social control and to organizational dynamics.

subject: SOCI
title: Sociology of War Crimes
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Sociological and cultural perspectives on war crimes; topics of responsibility, command responsibility, court-martial, and interrogation techniques; theories and concepts from forensic sociology applied to case studies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: SOCI
title: Social Entrepreneurship
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: Applying business principles and practices to solve social, economic and environmental problems; social entrepreneurship concepts and issues in scaling social enterprise ventures including management tools, organization structures, funding sources, impact measurement; experience in opportunity recognition, designing, planning, pitching social mission ventures; build social capital with social enterprise founders. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: MGMT 478 and PSAA 465 .

subject: SOCI
title: /MGMT 476 Entrepreneurship Practice
description: Practical skills for creating new businesses; evaluating, planning and operational strategy, including assessing the technology; product and service markets, value creation model; financing strategies; legal, regulatory, socio-economic drivers, risks; leadership to develop management team, advisory board; go-to-market strategy; develop own entrepreneurial opportunities or those of faculty and entrepreneurs. Cross Listing: MGMT 476/SOCI 476 .

title: Professional Development in Sociology I
prereq_text: Sociology major; junior or senior classification.

subject: SPMT
title: International Sport Business
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
description: Sport has evolved into a global industry, with organizations increasingly expanding into international markets to access new consumers, revenue streams and development opportunities. Given this shift, current and aspiring sport industry professionals must understand various aspects of international sport business, such as economic and legal environments, governance structures, cultural differences, communication styles, management practices and the strategic challenges associated with operating in the global marketplace. Case studies, lectures, scenarios and both individual and collaborative research projects introduce students to a range of international sports organizations (e.g., FIFA, IOC). Explore potential opportunities and issues, with a particular emphasis on examining distinctions between the U.S. sport industry and sport markets worldwide. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: TEFB
title: Introduction to Education in United States and Global Contexts
description: (EDUC 1301) Introduction to Education in United States and Global Contexts. This is a field-based course designed to introduce students to the structure and culture of schooling and classroom environments. The course emphasizes observation and analysis of educational settings through the lens of language, family engagement and academic background in local and global contexts. Students explore the educator’s role in supporting student learning and maintaining respectful learning environments.

subject: VTPB
title: Great Diseases of the World
prereq_text: Freshman or sophomore classification.
description: This course is designed to introduce you to major infectious diseases caused by viral, bacterial and parasitic pathogens that infect human beings, other mammals and sometimes insects. The lectures and assigned readings and videos focus on key historically important diseases, such as the plague, tuberculosis, cholera, influenza, yellow fever and HIV-AIDS, and recent emerging diseases, such as Ebola, Lassa Fever, COVID-19 and Monkey Pox. We will examine these diseases in depth, including their causes, historical impact, social and medical consequences, prevention and treatment. Prerequisite: Freshman or sophomore classification.

subject: VTPB
title: /RWFM 309 Wildlife Diseases
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.
description: This class provides an overview of diseases that affect wild mammals, birds, amphibians and reptiles. Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. They should be able to describe the signs of the disease, how it is transmitted, gross lesions, diagnostic criteria and prevention/control measures. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RWFM 309/VTPB 301 .

prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: This is an entry-level course designed to provide the students with an opportunity to gain an understanding of the basic features of the host defense system. The goal of this course is to familiarize the students with the mechanisms that are employed by the immune system to protect the host against infections and with the mechanisms that underlie aberrant immune responses including hypersensitivity reactions, autoimmune diseases and immune deficiency. subject: WGST
title: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course explores the core concepts of the interdisciplinary field of women’s and gender studies, focusing on various perspectives, scholarship, theories and histories of sex, gender and sexuality; examines theories of intersectionality, analyzing the interplay among race/racism, class/classism, sex/sexism, disability/ableism, nation/nationalism, religion/religious bias among other factors in gendered experiences and systems; surveys feminist, queer, anti-racist, decolonial and/or global scholarship that examines how social institutions and control mechanisms enact power, privilege and bias; engages controversial material and historical and/or contemporary case studies that challenge and/or support conventional understandings of gender, sex, sexuality, identity and power as necessary to achieve course learning outcomes and proficiency in disciplinary concepts and ideas. TOPICS. Course may include and is not limited to discussions and descriptions of violence, sexual assault, homophobia, transphobia, femicide, genocide, familial/domestic abuse, forced sterilization and workplace harassment; investigations of political controversies centered on reproductive and gender healthcare, gender identity, policing and/or immigration; analysis of popular culture and creative expression, including but not limited to: performance, literature, drag, music, visual culture; examinations of primary texts from historical and/or contemporary social movements and activists across the United States and around the globe; investigations of contemporary and historical labor relations and globalization; analyses and descriptions of anatomy, physiology and psychology. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives.

title: /SOCI 215 Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Studies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. The course focuses on current scholarship addressing the social construction of sex, sexuality and gender; institutional ways in which homophobia, biphobia and transphobia are systematically deployed; histories and examples of LGBTQ+ activism; evolution of desire and subjectivity; and the contributions of queer scholarship in understanding society. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings that address queer approaches to institutions; intersections of sexual and gender identity with race, class, ability/disability and/or nationality; digital activism; gender violence; controversies related to LGBTQ+ issues and politics, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Cross Listing: SOCI 215/WGST 205 .

subject: WGST
title: /SOCI 207 Introduction to Gender and Society
description: Explore the historical, cultural, social, economic and political dimensions of gender; define and distinguish gender roles and norms and identify sociological theories important to the study of gender; examine ideas and expectations about gender including historical and contemporary norms; understanding of scholarship on this topic increases intercultural competence and effective cross-cultural communication for participation in civic contexts and public life. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Cross Listing: SOCI 207/WGST 207 .

subject: WGST
title: /COMM 407 Gender, Race and Media
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity and related identities are produced, represented, negotiated, contested, consumed and/or performed in relation to media. Explores contributions of historically marginalized groups to media production, alongside analysis of how these groups have been portrayed as characters, audiences, communities and/or target markets. Focuses on media as a site of competing commercial, cultural, political, satirical and/or resistance narratives, rather than as a single, unified voice. Emphasizes critical interpretation of media texts and systems, while allowing space for multiple viewpoints and interpretations. Course material may include historical and contemporary examples that reflect both progress and controversy, analyzed for their cultural and communicative significance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages issues central to media literacy, political economy, representation and audience awareness in contemporary communication industries. Builds recognition of the ways portrayals of gender and race shape perception, credibility and/or trust in journalism, entertainment, advertising, representatives, community and public communication. Supports careers in communication, media industries, public relations, education, nonprofit work and leadership roles where navigating diverse audiences is essential. Supports informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts by highlighting how media representations influence identity, inclusion and public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that studying media portrayals of gender and race is not limited to celebration or criticism but involves examining how representation functions within broader cultural, social, economic, political and/or institutional systems. Illustrates how media are grounded in economies of production, representation and consumption across platforms, products and pipelines. Considers ways media might be empowering, stereotypical, commercial and/or transformative, depending on context, audience and community. Promotes awareness that interpretations of media content may differ across social, cultural and/or generational perspectives and that disagreement over meaning is part of scholarly analysis rather than a flaw in the material. Normalizes engagement with sensitive or contested topics as a means of understanding how media both reflect and shape public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media across film, television, news, advertising, music and digital platforms through production, representation and consumption; analysis of gender, race, ethnicity and intersectional identities in historical and contemporary contexts; consideration of media production practices, audience reception and the economic and institutional forces shaping representation; examination of stereotypes, invisibility, empowerment narratives and commercialized identity; discussion of how media both reinforce and challenge social norms related to power, privilege and belonging. Course material may include content that reflects real-world disparities or conflicting viewpoints. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 407/WGST 407 .

subject: WGST
title: /COMM 411 Representations of Motherhood
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. Course material may involve emotional and sensitive content such as depictions of grief, trauma, marginalization or public controversy as relevant to understanding how motherhood is framed in culture. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 411/WGST 411 .

title: /COMM 420 Gender and Communication

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how gender shapes and is shaped by communication across interpersonal, organizational and public contexts. Examines how people express, interpret and negotiate gender in everyday interaction, media environments and/or institutional settings. subject: WGST
title: /SOCI 455 Queer Theory
prereq_text: 6 hours in Women's and Gender Studies; senior classification or approval of instructor.
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course examines the field of queer theory as it emerged in the U.S. academy in the 1990s and grew and developed within and beyond U.S. borders in the early 21st century. The course includes scholarship on gender and sexual diversity and its overlaps with and divergences from feminist theories, while also highlighting the ways it functions as a critical practice that extends far beyond questions of gender and sexuality. Drawing on philosophy, literature, cultural studies and political theory, the course examines how “queer” operates as a challenge to systems of normalization — of identity, desire, embodiment and knowledge itself. The course considers foundational and contemporary texts in the field. TOPICS. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: 6 hours in Women's and Gender Studies; senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: SOCI 455/WGST 445 .

title: /HIST 473 Women in America Since 1877
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; HIST-473 also taught at Galveston campus.
description: CONTENT. History of women in the U.S. from the late 19th century to the present; role of intersectionality in defining the experience of modern womanhood; women as activists, workers, consumers, mothers and feminists; experiences, lives and influence of women of color; examination of contemporary social, political and economic histories. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; HIST-473 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: HIST 473/WGST 473 .
